text: Photothermal conditioning: mechanism and rationale: Photothermal conditioning involves the application of light at specific wavelengths (e.g. red or near-infrared) and mild heat to biological tissues or products like PRP. This process activates opsin receptors and transient receptor potential ion channels, triggering downstream G-protein signalling cascades that boost metabolic and secretory functions. The interaction between photons and cellular chromophores initiates a series of biochemical events that enhance cellular metabolism and promote the release of bioactive molecules. Photobiomodulation therapy results in increased ATP production and improved cellular metabolism as a result of photon absorption by mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase. This metabolic stimulation leads to increased protein synthesis, growth factor production and enhanced exosome secretion. In addition, the thermal component of the conditioning process further enhances the therapeutic cascade by improving enzyme activity and cellular transport. , Studies have shown that photothermal stimulation can significantly increase exosome and ATP release from PRP preparations and various cell types, without causing harm. For instance, the study by Mahmood et al . demonstrated that thermal stimulation at physiological temperatures increased exosome secretion without cytotoxic effects. text: Optimization parameters and standardization: Standardization of photothermal conditioning protocols is crucial for reproducible clinical results. However, it should be noted that several critical parameters such as wavelength selection, power density, exposure time and temperature control play a crucial role in the efficacy of photothermal conditioning. In biological tissues, red and near-infrared wavelengths (660–850 nm) have shown optimal penetration depth and biomodulator effects. Therefore, power density should be carefully controlled to achieve therapeutic effects without thermal damage to cellular components. , Temperature regulation during the conditioning process not only increases exosome production, but also plays an important role in preserving the viability and function of cellular components. The optimal temperature range of 37–42 °C is considered to enhance therapeutic benefits without compromising cellular integrity. Exposure time usually varies between 5 and 15 min, with 10 min being the most commonly used protocol. , , Factors such as ambient temperature, humidity and storage conditions can significantly affect the efficacy of the treatment. text: Example of commercial photothermal conditioning system: One example of a commercial photothermal conditioning platform is the MCT system (Meta Cell Technology, Barcelona, Spain), which has been designed to standardize PRP photothermal treatment through controlled electromagnetic and thermal energy exposure. The system applies specific wavelengths and controlled temperatures to PRP for a defined duration, typically 10 min. This process has been reported to increase growth factor release and exosome production in a more standard manner. Precise control of temperature, light exposure and duration are key features in photothermal platforms to ensure reproducibility in clinical applications. The systems also include real-time monitoring of operational parameters such as temperature and light intensity. , Photothermal PRP systems often use sterile, biocompatible containers engineered for light transparency and thermal stability. text: Abstract: Injectable aesthetic procedures are commonly discussed in terms of volumization, muscle relaxation, wrinkle reduction, and adverse events, whereas their potential effects on the dynamic mechanical environment of facial soft tissues have received less attention. The dermis is a mechanosensitive, viscoelastic tissue in which fibroblasts, extracellular matrix (ECM), interstitial fluid, vascular and lymphatic physiology, and repeated facial motion interact. Established evidence demonstrates that appropriately used hyaluronic acid fillers can restore structural support and stimulate collagen remodeling, while botulinum toxin reduces muscle contraction and dynamic rhytides. By contrast, direct clinical evidence that injectable procedures produce sustained abnormalities in tissue mechanics, lymphatic pumping, or mechanotransductive signaling remains limited. This narrative review integrates established clinical evidence, mechanistic evidence from adjacent fields, and hypothesis-generating interpretations to propose the concept of injectable procedure-related “mechanical silence”: a localized reduction or distortion of physiological tissue deformation, fluid exchange, and cell–matrix mechanical signaling. text: 1. Introduction: Dermal fillers and botulinum toxin are among the most frequently used minimally invasive aesthetic interventions. Their conventional clinical roles are straightforward: fillers replace or redistribute volume, improve contour, and support soft tissue; botulinum toxin reduces excessive or strategically selected muscle contraction and thereby improves dynamic rhytides. The mainstream literature has focused on efficacy, safety, injection anatomy, rheology, vascular complications, immunogenicity, and patient satisfaction [ , , , , , ]. However, aesthetic aging is also a mechanical phenomenon. Skin, subcutaneous fat, retaining ligaments, muscles, fascia, vessels, and lymphatics exist as a moving three-dimensional unit. Every facial expression, blink, smile, mastication cycle, sleep position, and postural change produces subtle tissue deformation. These repeated mechanical events are not merely external forces; they are biological signals interpreted by fibroblasts, endothelial cells, lymphatic endothelial cells, adipocytes, myocytes, immune cells, and keratinocytes. The hypothesis explored in this review is that injectable aesthetic procedures may alter this dynamic mechanical environment. In an ideal procedure, this alteration is beneficial: filler restores structural support to an atrophic or deflated compartment, and botulinum toxin reduces pathologic or aesthetically undesirable

This review uses the term mechanical silence to describe a local tissue state in which dynamic motion, fluid exchange, and cell–matrix deformation are reduced or replaced by persistent static pressure or chemical immobilization. The literature unrelated to the mechanistic questions of this review was not used to support clinical causal claims. For interpretation, the evidence was separated into three levels. The first level comprises established clinical observations, including filler-associated vascular complications, persistent edema, nodules and inflammatory reactions, as well as recognized botulinum-toxin effects such as paresis and muscle atrophy [ , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. The second level comprises mechanistic evidence showing that fibroblasts respond to matrix stiffness, stretch and cyclic loading; that lymph transport depends on intrinsic contractility and extrinsic mechanical forces; and that sustained tissue deformation can alter perfusion and tissue viability [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. The third level comprises the mechanical-silence hypothesis itself: the proposal that selected patterns of excessive or persistent filler-related loading or marked chemodenervation could alter local deformation, fluid exchange, or mechanotransductive signaling. This third level has not been established as a clinical adverse effect and requires prospective testing with objective mechanical, imaging, and physiological endpoints. summarizes this evidence hierarchy.

text: 3. Dermal Mechanobiology: Why Movement Matters: The dermis is a mechanosensitive organ. Fibroblasts attach to collagen, fibronectin, elastin-associated microfibrils, and other ECM molecules through integrins and focal adhesion complexes. Mechanical signals are transmitted through the cytoskeleton to the nucleus, where they influence gene expression, collagen production, matrix metalloproteinase activity, myofibroblast differentiation, and inflammatory signaling [ , , , , ]. The YAP/TAZ pathway is a central mechanotransductive regulator, responding to tissue stiffness, cell shape, and cytoskeletal tension [ ]. Substrate stiffness can direct stem-cell lineage specification, and by extension, dermal stiffness can influence fibroblast phenotype, myofibroblast activation, and ECM production [ , ]. In young and healthy skin, fibroblasts are elongated and mechanically engaged with an organized collagen network. In aged or photoaged skin, collagen fragmentation reduces mechanical tension, leading to fibroblast collapse, reduced procollagen synthesis, increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, and a self-perpetuating cycle of matrix deterioration [ , , , , ]. This observation is critical for aesthetic medicine: dermal quality depends not only on adding material or reducing movement but also on restoring appropriate mechanical information to cells. Too little mechanical tension may lead to cellular inactivity; excessive or abnormal

Skin behaves as a heterogeneous, hydrated viscoelastic tissue in which the collagen–elastin network provides a major solid structural framework, while proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, bound water, and mobile interstitial fluid contribute to time-dependent deformation and load redistribution. Consequently, mechanical loading produces not only instantaneous deformation but also creep, stress relaxation, and fluid redistribution over time. Proteoglycan-rich ground substance is particularly relevant because its interaction with water contributes to tissue hydration, matrix spacing, and transmission of mechanical loads between the fibrillar ECM and the interstitial fluid phase. From this perspective, an injectable material may change not only static stiffness but also local relaxation behavior, tissue recoil, interstitial pressure, and fluid movement. More broadly, viscoelastic biomaterial studies demonstrate that cellular mechanosensing can depend on the relationship between matrix relaxation timescale and cell-adhesion dynamics [ ]. text: 4. Dermal Fillers: Beneficial Support Versus Chronic Mass Effect: Hyaluronic acid fillers are not biologically inert. Clinical and histological studies indicate that cross-linked hyaluronic acid can integrate into dermal tissue, alter local mechanics, stimulate fibroblast elongation, and induce new collagen production [ , , , ]. This effect is often beneficial because photodamaged skin contains fragmented collagen and collapsed fibroblasts. By restoring mechanical stretch, a well-placed filler can re-engage fibroblasts and partially restore a youthful matrix environment [ , , , , , , ]. Thus, the proposed mechanical-silence hypothesis should not be confused with a blanket anti-filler argument. The concern arises when filler becomes excessive, persistent, poorly distributed, or positioned in a region with limited drainage capacity. Filler has rheological properties such as elasticity, cohesivity, swelling behavior, viscosity, and resistance to deformation. These properties determine how a product spreads, integrates, displaces tissue, resists compression, and interacts with the surrounding ECM. A small amount of filler in the correct plane may restore support, whereas repeated injections in a superficial or lymphatic-rich region may create a persistent mass that changes pressure gradients and tissue mobility. Cross-linked HA products are hydrated viscoelastic gels that provide immediate volume and load sharing, with product-specific differences in elasticity, viscosity, cohesivity, swelling behavior, and tissue integration [ , , , ]. From a mechanobiological perspective, excessive filler may influence three linked processes. First, it may change the deformation pattern of the ECM. Instead of allowing the tissue to expand and recoil freely, a bolus or sheet of filler may impose constant stretch, compression, or stiffness. Second, it may alter interstitial fluid movement. Lymphatic capillaries are low-pressure structures that can be affected by tissue deformation and pressure gradients; lymphatic dysfunction has been observed in compressed skin models [ ]. Third, filler may modify vascular flow. In the most serious setting, intravascular or perivascular filler can cause vascular occlusion, skin necrosis, or blindness [ , , , ]. In less severe settings, persistent pressure or edema may contribute to microcirculatory inefficiency, although this requires direct measurement. It is useful to distinguish regenerative mechanical stretch from maladaptive static deformation. Wang and colleagues showed that cross-linked hyaluronic acid in photodamaged skin stimulated collagen synthesis and produced stretched, biosynthetically active fibroblasts [ ]. Botulinum Toxin: Dynamic Wrinkle Control and the Question of Mechanical Quiescence: Botulinum toxin type A acts primarily by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction through cleavage of SNAP-25 and disruption of SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion [ , , , ]. In aesthetic medicine, this produces temporary reduction in muscle contraction and improvement of dynamic wrinkles. The desired effect is movement modulation, not tissue destruction. In clinical practice, precise dosing can reduce excessive contraction while preserving natural expression. The mechanobiological question is different. If repeated or high-dose chemodenervation substantially reduces muscle activity, the overlying skin and subcutaneous tissue may receive less cyclic movement. Facial muscles are not merely wrinkle-generating structures; they also create local tissue deformation, contribute to venous and lymphatic movement, and transmit mechanical information to the dermis through fascial, ligamentous, and cutaneous insertions. Reduction in contraction may therefore reduce both unwanted wrinkle-forming compression and potentially useful low-amplitude mechanical stimulation. Evidence from the skeletal muscle literature shows that botulinum toxin-induced paralysis can produce muscle atrophy and molecular changes related to denervation [ , ]. More recent studies have explored differences between botulinum toxin paralysis and neurectomy in fibrosis, NF-kB, and TGF-beta signaling [ ].

text: 6. Lymphatic Drainage, Vascular Circulation, and Facial Motion: The lymphatic system maintains interstitial-fluid balance, immune surveillance, lipid transport, and macromolecule clearance. Unlike the arterial circulation, lymphatic flow depends on intrinsic lymphatic contractility, pressure gradients, valves, respiration, arterial pulsation, and extrinsic tissue movement [ , , , , , ]. In the face, thin tissues, repeated blinking, facial muscle contraction, and gravity-dependent postural changes likely contribute to fluid redistribution. The periorbital and malar regions are particularly susceptible to visible fluid accumulation because of thin skin, ligamentous boundaries, age-related tissue laxity, venous anatomy, and lymphatic complexity. Fillers and botulinum toxin could influence this system through different mechanisms. Fillers may create a physical volume, hydrophilic reservoir, or local stiffness that changes interstitial-fluid pressure and lymphatic clearance. Botulinum toxin may reduce the extrinsic muscle-motion component of lymphatic flow. Both may interact with venous drainage: filler may contribute to venous stasis or local pressure in certain planes, while botulinum toxin may either reduce vasoconstrictive tone or increase perfusion in selected settings [ ]. Therefore, the direction of effect is not uniform. Pressure-injury biology provides only a limited conceptual analogy. Sustained tissue deformation can impair perfusion,

Molecular Pathways Potentially Affected by Reduced ECM Expansion and Recoil: The phrase ECM expansion and contraction refers to the repeated deformation of collagen, elastin, ground substance, and interstitial-fluid spaces during normal tissue motion. At the cellular level, these events are sensed through integrins, focal adhesion kinase, talin, vinculin, stretch-activated ion channels, the actin cytoskeleton, nuclear lamins, and transcriptional regulators such as YAP and TAZ [ , , , , , , , , ]. Mechanical input also interacts with growth-factor signaling. TGF-beta can be stored in a latent ECM-bound form, and mechanical tension can affect its activation; myofibroblast differentiation is similarly linked to matrix stiffness, actomyosin tension, and alpha-smooth-muscle-actin expression [ , ]. Therefore, the dermis receives biochemical signals partly because it is mechanically deformed. A filler placed in the dermis or subcutaneous tissue can alter this signaling in two opposite directions. When it restores lost tension to fragmented collagen, it may improve fibroblast spreading and matrix synthesis [ , ]. When it produces focal stiffness, chronic swelling, or a poorly mobile gel-tissue interface, it may reduce the normal pattern of cyclic strain. In that setting, fibroblasts may receive a constant static signal instead of physiologic oscillatory input. Botulinum toxin affects the same system from the opposite direction. It does not add a physical mass, but it reduces the movement generator. In the upper face, glabellar complex, orbicularis oculi, frontalis, mentalis, depressor anguli oris, and platysma, muscle contraction repeatedly changes dermal strain. Controlled reduction in hypercontraction reduces repeated folding, which is beneficial. Excessive reduction may lower tissue deformation below a biologically useful range. This is similar to the difference between correcting harmful overuse and inducing disuse. Disuse biology is well recognized in skeletal muscle, where loss of activity is linked to atrophy, altered gene expression, and changes in connective tissue [ , , ]. The facial dermis is not skeletal muscle, but it is mechanically coupled to muscle. This section proposes a hypothetical U-shaped mechanobiological framework for future investigation. text: 8. Clinical Phenotypes That Could Be Reinterpreted Through the Mechanical-Silence Framework: Several clinical observations can be used to generate, but not confirm, the mechanical-silence hypothesis. Persistent malar or periorbital edema after HA filler is an established clinical phenomenon, with proposed contributors including product hydrophilicity, injection plane, anatomy, inflammation, venous factors, and lymphatic susceptibility [ , , , ]. Whether altered tissue deformation or reduced muscle-generated motion independently contributes to this edema has not been demonstrated. Likewise, cumulative filler burden may be associated clinically with palpable firmness, overcorrection, altered contour, or reduced apparent mobility, but a direct causal relationship between cumulative filler exposure and abnormal mechanotransductive signaling has not been established. Other observations—including prolonged swelling after subsequent procedures or a subjective mismatch between wrinkle reduction and natural facial animation—are even less specific and may have multiple alternative explanations. These phenomena should therefore not be regarded as manifestations of a defined mechanical-silence syndrome. Their relevance is primarily hypothesis-generating: they identify patient groups in whom objective measurements of filler burden, tissue stiffness, dynamic deformation, perfusion, and regional fluid clearance could be particularly informative.

Proposed Concept: Injectable Procedure-Related Mechanical Silence: For the purposes of this review, injectable procedure-related mechanical silence is defined as a hypothetical local state characterized by a measurable reduction or distortion of normal dynamic tissue deformation, rather than as a recognized diagnosis or established complication. Potential contributing variables include persistent local stiffness or mass effect, reduced expansion–recoil cycles, altered interstitial-fluid movement, or marked reduction in muscle-driven tissue excursion. The proposed construct therefore requires operational measurement before it can be assigned clinical significance. Candidate mechanical endpoints include dynamic strain amplitude during standardized facial movement, deformation and recoil measured over repeated loading cycles, regional stiffness measured by elastography, superficial skin distensibility and elastic recovery, muscle excursion, and the relationship between filler burden and movement of adjacent soft-tissue layers. Candidate physiological endpoints include lymphatic transit, regional perfusion, edema volume, and interstitial-fluid-related imaging findings. Molecular or translational studies could additionally evaluate focal-adhesion signaling, YAP/TAZ localization, cytoskeletal organization, and ECM-remodeling markers. Importantly, no validated facial-skin strain threshold currently defines YAP/TAZ inactivation or “mechanical silence”

Within this framework, HA-dominant, chemodenervation-dominant, and combined exposure patterns can be investigated separately because they represent different mechanical perturbations. HA may change local volume, hydration, stiffness, or deformation patterns, whereas botulinum toxin primarily changes the active movement generator. CaHA and PLLA require separate interpretation because their particulate and biostimulatory behavior differs from that of HA. These relationships remain hypotheses until longitudinal human studies demonstrate reproducible associations between injectable exposure and objective mechanical or physiological endpoints. The framework is therefore intended to generate testable research questions, not to define a new adverse-event diagnosis or treatment indication.

text: Abstract: Abstract Background Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) is widely used in aesthetic dermatology, particularly for dynamic wrinkles in the upper facial third. Beyond cosmetic effects, BoNT-A may influence emotional processing through the skin-brain axis. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on psychological and psychiatric outcomes of upper facial BoNT-A treatment, with a focus on mechanisms extending beyond aesthetics. Methods A structured search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through January 2026. Search terms included “botulinum toxin,” “upper facial third,” “psychodermatology,” “facial feedback,” “depression,” “anxiety,” and “psychiatric disorders.” Original studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses assessing psychological, psychiatric, or neurobiological outcomes were included. Results Upper facial BoNT-A is associated with clinically meaningful reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms, and improvements in self-perception and social functioning. Inhibition of corrugator and procerus muscles modulates afferent signaling to limbic structures, supporting the facial feedback hypothesis. text: Introduction: Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) has become established as one of the most widely used medical treatments worldwide, especially in aesthetic dermatology ( ). In the cosmetic field, its use in the upper facial third, primarily for the treatment of glabellar, forehead, and periorbital lines, represents one of the most frequent minimally invasive interventions in dermatology and aesthetic medicine ( , ). Beyond its demonstrated efficacy in reducing dynamic wrinkles and improving facial appearance, the impact of botulinum toxin treatment transcends the purely aesthetic realm, influencing emotional, psychological, and social dimensions of the patient ( – ). In recent decades, the perception of facial aesthetics has acquired growing relevance in quality of life, self-esteem, and social interaction. The face constitutes a central element in emotional communication and in the construction of personal identity, such that alterations in its expression can have significant repercussions on psychological well-being ( ). In this context, the improvement of facial appearance through aesthetic treatments is associated not only with visible physical changes, but also with modifications in self-perception, mood, and personal confidence ( – ). text: Methods: This study was conducted as a narrative review of the literature addressing the psychodermatological effects of BoNT-A applied to the upper facial third. text: Relevant sections: The skin-brain axis constitutes a broad conceptual framework that describes the bidirectional communication between the central nervous system and the skin, mediated by neuroendocrine, immunological, and peripheral pathways ( – ). The skin functions not only as a physical barrier but also as a neuroimmunoendocrine organ capable of perceiving and transmitting emotional signals ( , ). Specialized cutaneous receptors capture tactile, painful, or temperature stimuli and transmit them via afferent fibers to the spinal cord and brainstem, connecting with limbic system structures such as the amygdala and cingulate cortex, which process emotion and emotional memory ( ). Additionally, the skin can release neurotransmitters and cytokines that modulate inflammation, pain perception, and stress response ( , ). Psychodermatology studies these interactions and how psychological factors can influence cutaneous diseases, as well as how skin alterations affect mental health ( , ). This framework provides the foundation for understanding how interventions that modulate facial expression, such as botulinum toxin, can impact not only appearance but also the organism’s emotional and stress circuits ( ).

text: Facial feedback and emotional modulation: Within the skin-brain axis, the facial feedback theory offers a specific mechanism by which facial muscle activity contributes to the generation and regulation of emotions ( , ). The muscles of the forehead and glabellar region, when contracted, send proprioceptive information through the trigeminal nerve to brainstem nuclei and limbic system structures, including the amygdala, insula, and prefrontal cortex, modulating the perception of emotional states such as anger, tension, or sadness ( , ). The temporary inhibition of these muscles through botulinum toxin alters these afferent stimuli, decreasing the activation of limbic circuits associated with negative emotions and favoring more relaxed and positive emotional states ( ). This neurophysiological mechanism demonstrates that the modification of facial expression is not limited to aesthetic effect but directly influences emotional experience and the regulation of anxiety and mood ( – ).

text: Botulinum toxin in the upper facial third: mechanisms and clinical applications: Botulinum toxin type A acts by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing temporary paralysis of innervated muscles ( , ). In the upper facial third, it primarily affects the corrugator, frontalis, and orbicularis oculi muscles, responsible for dynamic expression lines in the forehead, glabella, and periocular region ( , ). These structures not only contribute to aesthetics but also participate directly in emotional expression and in the transmission of proprioceptive information to the limbic system, integrating the functional dimension with aesthetics ( ). The precise application of the toxin allows modulation of muscle activity without compromising natural expression, optimizing the balance between visual effects and influence on emotional circuits ( ). Factors such as dose, injection technique, and patient selection are fundamental to maximizing results and minimizing adverse effects ( , ).

Although BoNT-A is not indicated as a primary treatment for psychiatric disorders, accumulating evidence suggests that modulation of facial muscle activity may influence emotional processing and social behavior through mechanisms related to the skin-brain axis and facial feedback pathways ( , , ). text: Psychological and psychiatric outcomes associated with botulinum toxin treatment: psychiatric endpoints. Given the variability in the strength and quality of evidence across diagnostic categories, the following sections summarize findings accordingly. Evidence from meta-analyses, systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and observational studies has reported reductions in depressive symptom severity following BoNT-A injections in the glabellar region ( – , , , , ). The proposed mechanism centers on the facial feedback hypothesis, whereby inhibition of corrugator and procerus muscle activity reduces negative afferent signaling to limbic structures such as the amygdala and insula ( , ). Evidence indicates that the specific site of injection may influence emotional outcomes, with differences observed between glabellar, frontalis, and combined applications. This highlights the importance of anatomical targeting within the facial feedback pathway ( ). Additional contributory factors include improvements in self-image, reduced perception of negative social feedback, and enhanced interpersonal engagement ( , ). text: Anxiety disorders: Several studies have reported reductions in anxiety-related symptoms following botulinum toxin treatment in the upper facial third ( , , ). Decreased activation of facial muscles associated with fear, concern, or anger may reduce afferent input to limbic and autonomic centers involved in anxiety regulation, contributing to subjective feelings of calm and emotional control ( , , ). Regarding Social Anxiety Disorder, by softening expressions associated with tension or worry, BoNT-A treatment may reduce perceived social threat and facilitate more positive interpersonal interactions ( , ). Improved facial appearance and expressivity may also influence social feedback loops, reinforcing self-confidence and reducing avoidance behaviors ( , ). Beyond these mechanisms, preliminary observations suggest that BoNT−A may directly alleviate social anxiety symptoms in broader populations. Improvements in interpersonal functioning and perceived social threat have been reported, although data remain limited and require confirmation in controlled studies ( ). While direct evidence remains limited, these mechanisms suggest a plausible adjunctive role for botulinum toxin in socially mediated anxiety symptoms ( , ).

text: Personality traits and disorders: Theoretical models suggest that modulation of facial feedback may influence emotional intensity and interpersonal signaling in individuals with certain personality traits ( , , ). By reducing exaggerated facial expressions associated with anger, distress, or tension, BoNT-A may contribute to improved emotional regulation and social interaction in selected cases ( , , ). However, patients with personality traits may present increased vulnerability to unrealistic expectations or dissatisfaction with aesthetic outcomes ( , ). Consequently, the use of botulinum toxin in this population requires heightened clinical caution, clear therapeutic boundaries, and close collaboration with mental health professionals ( , ).

text: Body dysmorphic disorder: Particular caution is warranted in patients with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), as these individuals frequently seek cosmetic procedures, including botulinum toxin type A, yet these interventions rarely result in sustained psychological improvement ( , ). Moreover, the presence of unrealistic expectations or excessive preoccupation with perceived defects has been associated with persistent dissatisfaction, repeated treatment-seeking, and poor psychosocial outcomes in aesthetic populations ( , , ). Therefore, BoNT-A should not be considered a therapeutic strategy for BDD, and careful psychiatric evaluation and referral are essential when body image pathology is suspected ( , ).

text: Discussion: This narrative review highlights that botulinum toxin type A (BoNT−A) injections in the upper facial third exert psychodermatological effects that extend beyond aesthetic enhancement, influencing emotional processing, affective symptoms, and social functioning. Evidence from randomized controlled trials ( ) suggests that BoNT-A may reduce depressive symptom severity, with several studies demonstrating statistically significant improvements compared with placebo ( – , ). Meta−analyses further support a modest but consistent antidepressant effect ( , , ). However, these findings require cautious interpretation, as most trials are limited by small sample sizes, short follow−up periods, and heterogeneity in inclusion criteria and psychiatric outcome measures ( , ). Beyond depression, emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for anxiety−related symptoms, particularly in socially mediated contexts. Observational studies and small controlled trials have reported reductions in anxiety levels and improvements in social confidence following BoNT−A treatment ( , , ), although the strength of evidence remains weaker than that for depressive disorders ( ). Data regarding bipolar disorder and personality disorders are preliminary and heterogeneous, consisting mainly of small trials, case series, or exploratory neuroimaging studies ( , , , , ), which precludes firm conclusions.

text: Discussion: Mechanistically, the psychotropic effects of BoNT−A are supported by converging preclinical and human evidence. Preclinical studies demonstrate that modulation of peripheral sensory input can influence central stress and emotional circuits through neuroimmune and neuroendocrine pathways within the skin-brain axis ( , , ). In humans, functional neuroimaging studies provide more direct support: inhibition of corrugator muscle activity via BoNT−A has been associated with reduced amygdala activation during the processing of negative emotional stimuli ( , , ). These findings offer neurobiological validation of the facial feedback hypothesis, suggesting that peripheral modulation of facial musculature can translate into measurable changes in limbic system activity. Psychosocial mechanisms likely act in parallel with these biological pathways. Improvements in self−perception, attenuation of negative facial expressions, and changes in social feedback loops may reinforce emotional regulation and contribute to the overall therapeutic effect ( , , ). The interplay between neurobiological and psychosocial factors supports a biopsychosocial model of BoNT−A action within psychodermatology. Despite these promising findings, several methodological limitations must be emphasized. Most randomized controlled trials include small samples, limiting statistical power and external validity ( , ).

text: Discussion: Considerable heterogeneity exists across studies in terms of patient populations, injection protocols, and psychiatric outcome measures, complicating direct comparisons ( , ). Observational studies, while informative, are particularly susceptible to selection bias and confounding ( , ). A specific methodological challenge in BoNT−A research is functional unblinding. Because the muscular effects of BoNT−A are visible and perceptible, participants may correctly infer their treatment allocation, introducing expectancy bias and potentially inflating subjective improvements in mood or anxiety ( , ). This limitation is inherent to the mechanism of action of BoNT−A and must be considered when interpreting placebo−controlled trials. Clinically, current evidence suggests that BoNT−A may serve as an adjunctive intervention in selected patients, particularly those with mild−to−moderate depressive symptoms, social anxiety features, or heightened emotional reactivity ( ). However, it should not replace established psychiatric treatments. Careful patient selection remains essential, especially in individuals with body dysmorphic disorder, maladaptive personality traits, or unrealistic expectations, where aesthetic interventions may be contraindicated or require psychiatric co−management ( , ). Clinicians trained to identify psychiatric comorbidities and manage psychosocial expectations may enhance both safety and outcomes in patients undergoing BoNT−A treatment. Overall, while current evidence supports the psychodermatological relevance of BoNT−A, larger, well−designed randomized controlled trials with standardized psychiatric and neurobiological endpoints are needed to clarify its therapeutic potential and define its role within clinical practice.

text: Limitations: Several limitations of the available evidence should be noted. First, the narrative review methodology, while appropriate given the heterogeneity of included studies, does not permit quantitative synthesis of effect sizes or formal assessment of publication bias. Second, included studies vary substantially in design, sample size, patient population, injection site, dosing protocols, and psychiatric outcome measures, limiting direct comparability. Third, most RCTs are small, and many observational studies rely on self-reported outcomes without blinded assessment. Fourth, the absence of standardized psychiatric endpoints across studies makes it difficult to draw definitive conclusions regarding the magnitude and durability of psychodermatological effects. Fifth, the present review was limited to English-language publications, which may introduce language bias. These limitations reinforce the need for large, well-designed, prospective RCTs with standardized psychiatric endpoints as a priority for future research.

text: Conclusions: Botulinum toxin type A applied to the upper facial third demonstrates psychodermatological effects that extend meaningfully beyond aesthetic improvement. Current evidence supports its role in modulating emotional processing through facial feedback mechanisms within the skin-brain axis, contributing to reductions in depressive symptoms, attenuation of anxiety, and improvements in self-perception and social functioning. BoNT-A should be considered a complementary intervention within a broader biopsychosocial framework rather than a primary psychiatric treatment. Future large-scale RCTs with standardized psychiatric and neurobiological outcome measures, longitudinal neuroimaging studies, and investigation of dose-response relationships and individual moderators will be essential to consolidate the evidence base and enable more personalized clinical application within psychodermatology.

Longitudinal neuroimaging studies are needed to further elucidate causal mechanisms linking peripheral muscle modulation to limbic activity over time. Investigation of dose-response relationships, optimal injection intervals, and individual moderators such as baseline symptom severity, personality traits, and biological sex may facilitate more personalized and evidence-based application within psychodermatology.

text: Abstract: Abstract More aesthetic patients now ask for changes in facial contour: a smaller face, a sharper jawline, and less sagging. Botulinum toxin (BoNT) is best known as a treatment for wrinkles, but it can also be used for modifying facial contour. With BoNT alone, a wide face can be made narrower, a heavy lower face can be made lighter, sagging on the jawline can be reduced, and a short chin can be corrected. Many physicians already do this, but each site is taught and studied on its own. This review brings the sites together under the name “contouring BoNT”. It describes seven sites: five muscles (masseter, temporalis, platysma, depressor anguli oris, mentalis) and two salivary glands (parotid, submandibular). The seven sites work in three ways: reducing the volume of a muscle or gland, removing a downward pull so that the face looks lifted, and relaxing an overactive muscle that changes the shape of the chin. All three serve one goal that patients describe in their own words: a smaller and lifted face. For each site, the review explains what it does to the contour, who is a good candidate, who needs caution, the published dose range and the authors’ practice, and which neighboring site changes when the target is treated. It explains which sites are checked together and how each is examined. Two safety points specific to contouring—the immunogenicity of large repeated doses, and

text: 1. Introduction: More and more aesthetic patients are requesting changes in facial contour, wanting a smaller face, a sharper jawline, less sagging of the lower face, or the correction of a short chin. This includes the large group who ask for “lifting” or “tightening”. Facial contour has become one of the main reasons for visiting an aesthetic clinic. In BoNT, this change is reflected in regulatory activity in the United States: platysma bands, a neck contour indication, were approved by the FDA in 2024 [ ], and masseter muscle prominence is under FDA review after two phase 3 trials [ ]. These approvals are specific to the United States; neither indication is approved in most other jurisdictions. Contour deserves this attention. It is a large part of what makes a face look young or old. Studies of perceived age consistently rank sagging and facial shape together with wrinkles as signs of age, across ethnic groups [ , , ]. In a recent study of East Asian women, the strongest signs of age were the nasolabial fold, the marionette fold, and a loss of contour tightness [ ]. These are features of contour, not skin. A treatment that improves contour improves perceived age, even if it does not touch a wrinkle. Patients know masseter BoNT well. Few know that BoNT can change other parts of the contour, and many physicians still think of it mainly as a wrinkle treatment. For the physician, it is a strong

Filler, threads, and energy devices add volume, lift tissue, or tighten skin; BoNT works on a different part of the problem, and the treatments complement each other. For patients whose contour problem is mainly a large muscle or gland, BoNT alone produces most of the desired result, quickly, at low cost, with no downtime, and reversibly. This is not a small group. In a survey of 469 Korean dermatologists, masseter treatment was among the most requested BoNT indications, and it was most popular in patients in their twenties and thirties [ ]. The other sites in this review are treated for the same reason every day. The literature on these sites is rich but scattered. There is a systematic review on the masseter, for which a phase 3 program is also underway. The temporalis, parotid gland, submandibular gland, depressor anguli oris, platysma and mentalis each have their own smaller literature, usually reviewed alone [ , , , , ], and a recent review of contouring with neuromodulators covered the masseter, temporalis, and parotid [ ]. text: 2. Methods: This is a narrative review. We searched PubMed and Scopus from inception to September 2026 for clinical, anatomical, imaging, and safety studies of botulinum toxin injection into the masseter, temporalis, parotid gland, submandibular gland, depressor anguli oris, platysma, and mentalis for facial contour. The search terms combined “botulinum toxin” or “botulinum neurotoxin” with each site name and with “facial contouring”, “facial slimming”, “jawline”, “chin”, and “temple”. Reference lists of retrieved articles, consensus statements, and regulatory documents were searched by hand. We included randomized trials, prospective and retrospective studies, case series, case reports, anatomical and imaging studies, and consensus statements in English that addressed one of the seven sites as a contouring target or its safety. Studies of these sites for other indications (wrinkles, bruxism, pain, sialorrhea) were used only where they gave dose, safety, or volume data relevant to contouring. No formal quality scoring was applied; the type of evidence available for each site is summarized in . The selection logic of the framework—who is a good candidate, who needs caution, and which sites are checked together—comes from the authors’ clinical practice in an East Asian population. It is labeled as the authors’ practice or observation wherever it appears, and it is proposed for prospective

text: 3. How the Seven Sites Work: The seven sites were chosen based on three criteria: the structure shapes the contour of the face at rest; BoNT changes it in a way that is seen and reproducible in practice; and there is at least some published support for its use as a contouring target. Other structures were considered and left out. The buccinator and the lip elevators were excluded because weakening them harms oral function or facial expression for little contour gain. The risorius was excluded because its contour effect is small and the evidence is limited to anecdotes. Other facial muscles shape expression or wrinkles rather than the resting contour and were not considered. The list is therefore a practical checklist, not a complete map of the face, and it may grow as evidence grows. Reduce. BoNT makes the injected structure smaller. There are four sites: two muscles, the masseter and the temporalis, and two glands, the parotid and the submandibular. The masseter and parotid make the lower face wide; the temporalis makes the upper face wide; the submandibular gland blurs the line between the jaw and neck. Rebalance. BoNT turns off a muscle that pulls down, so that the muscles that pull up win. Two sites work as one system: the platysma and the depressor anguli oris. text: 4. The Seven Sites: summarizes the evidence available for each site. It differs widely: randomized trials and a phase 3 program have investigated the masseter; one randomized trial and prospective series have been conducted on the parotid; for the platysma, randomized trials have been conducted for bands and one prospective study for the jawline; the temporalis, submandibular gland, depressor anguli oris, and mentalis rest on small series, anatomical studies, and consensus. In the paragraphs that follow, “published doses” are the doses reported in the cited studies, with the product named there. “The authors use” refers to the authors’ starting doses in East Asian patients; these represent expert practice, not trial evidence, and they are not expected to transfer unchanged to other populations. Of the neighboring-site effects described under “What to watch”, the temporalis response to masseter treatment is documented in trials; the others are the authors’ observations. What it does. The masseter often forms the lateral boundary of the lower face in front of the mandibular angle. When it is large, the lower face looks square and heavy from the front. Reducing it narrows the lower face; a prospective pilot study using 3D surface measurement in 11 patients found the masseter area to be smaller at 1 month and still reduced at 3 months [ ]. text: 4. The Seven Sites: reviews of technique and safety [ , ] and a phase 3 program under regulatory review [ ]. Who is a good candidate. A patient whose lower-face boundary is muscle. This must be confirmed, not assumed. Ask the patient to clench; the masseter hardens, and the boundary becomes more prominent. Feel it with both hands. Younger patients with firm skin respond best because the skin follows the shrinking muscle. The first group has a wide lower face that is not mainly masseter. From the front, the lateral boundary may be formed by cheek soft tissue in front of the masseter ( ) or by the parotid gland behind it. Masseter BoNT does little for either; the parotid needs its own treatment ( ), and cheek soft tissue is not a BoNT target. The second group has loose skin. If the masseter shrinks quickly and the skin cannot follow, the result is jowl sagging, or a visible step at the anterior border of the masseter where the treated muscle meets untreated cheek. The third group has a pre-existing lateral cheek hollow. If the cheek above the masseter already lacks volume, reducing the masseter also removes the volume below it, and the patient says that the cheek “sank” after treatment. This happens more when injections are placed high. Inject low, toward the jawline. How. The published doses are mostly 20–30 U per side. The authors use 10–20 U per side, 3–4 points. The temporalis. text: 4. The Seven Sites: triple-blind trial found that patients who received a second masseter injection at 3 months had a thicker temporalis on ultrasound and higher temporalis EMG activity at 6 months than patients who received saline [ ]. A later study found that the temporalis thickness rose from 9.3 to 13.1 mm at rest after masseter BoNT [ ]. The practical rule: check the temporalis in every masseter candidate at baseline, and again at follow-up in patients treated repeatedly. If the temporalis is already large and bulges on clenching, treating both can be considered; otherwise, explain what may happen and reassess the temporalis at follow-up. The decision is made for each patient, not as a rule. The patient who no longer needs it. After repeated treatment, the masseter often does not return to its original size, even long after the last injection [ , ]. Once this happens, treatment does not need to be repeated on schedule. In the authors’ experience, some patients nevertheless ask for it again and again while the muscle is no longer large. They should be examined and told when there is nothing left to reduce.

text: 4.2. Temporalis: What it does. The temporalis forms the lateral boundary of the upper face. When it is large, the forehead looks wide, and the face takes an inverted-triangle shape. Reducing it narrows the upper face ( C,D). The circumference of the upper face decreases measurably after temporalis BoNT [ ]. Who is a good candidate. Three groups. The first group is patients with an inverted-triangle face and a visible temporal bulge on clenching. The second group is every masseter candidate, as a baseline check ( ). The third group is patients asking for a smaller face in general. A useful clue: many women with a large temporalis wear their hair down over the temples. They usually know about the problem before the physician does. Repeated masseter-only treatment in a patient with a large temporalis makes the inverted triangle worse over time. This is the clearest reason to assess the two muscles together. Who needs caution. The patient with a temple hollow—not because BoNT is wrong for them, but because the two treatments of the temple go to different places. The hollow lies in the lower front part of the temporal fossa, where the surface layers are mainly fascia and fat over a thin, tendinous part of the muscle [ ]; this is where filler goes. The muscle belly that BoNT treats lies higher and further back. Injecting low, in the hollow zone, does not narrow the face and can make the hollow look

text: 4.2. Temporalis: deeper, so the authors avoid it unless that area bulges on chewing. How. The published doses vary widely and are mostly higher than those below [ , ]. The authors use 10–20 U per side, 4–5 points, into the muscle belly. What to watch. Hollowing, when injections are placed too low, or the belly is over-reduced. Headache and chewing fatigue are uncommon. An observation not previously reported. In patients who want temple filler for a hollow temple, the authors first check the temporalis muscle above the hollow. The hollow is partly a step between the hollow zone and the muscle belly above and behind it. When the belly is large, the step is deep and the hollow looks worse than its true volume loss. Reducing the belly with BoNT softens the step, and the amount of filler needed is then smaller—which matters, because filler placed in contour areas enlarges the face, and temple filler can require up to 2 mL per side [ ]. It is established that temporalis size sets the outline of the upper face. The use of temporalis BoNT to reduce the amount of temple filler is the authors’ clinical observation; it has not been tested in a study.

text: 4.3. Parotid Gland: What it does. The parotid sits behind the masseter, in front of and below the ear. When it is large, it forms part of the lateral boundary of the lower face, and it is often the real cause of a face that looks square but does not respond to masseter BoNT. BoNT reduces it: a randomized trial with high-dose, low-dose, and placebo arms found significant volume reduction in both treated arms, with recovery of only 5–8% at 3 months [ ], and prospective series confirm the effect [ , ]. Who is a good candidate. A patient whose parotid is enlarged, whether or not the masseter is also large. When both are large, both are treated ( A,B). When only the masseter is treated in such a patient, the parotid becomes the new boundary, and the face looks no narrower. The gland does not harden on clenching and is soft on palpation with both hands. Population MRI data explain who these patients are: the mean parotid volume was 27.8 cm 3 in men and 21.6 cm 3 in women, and the volume rose with body mass index, age, and male sex [ ]. In the authors’ experience, the pattern is clear: the gland is largest in overweight, older men. There is one note on expectations. In overweight patients, part of the gland enlargement is fat, not secretory tissue. The parotid fat fraction rose from 30% in underweight to 47% in overweight subjects on MRI [ ]. BoNT causes the atrophy of secretory tissue and does not

text: 4.3. Parotid Gland: remove fat. A larger gland needs a larger dose, and the secretory part will shrink in proportion. But the fat will not, so the gland does not shrink as much as its size suggests. The patient should be told this before treatment. Who needs caution. A patient with a gland that is not clinically evident. How. Published protocols vary in dose and point number [ , , ]. The authors use 15–40 U per side, higher in very large glands. The number of points follows the shape of the enlargement: 2–3 points when only the part in front of the ear is prominent, and 5–8 points when both the parts in front of and below the ear are enlarged. Ultrasound guidance is advisable, particularly for less experienced injectors ( ). A practical point: the gland stands out more when the patient lies back, so the authors inject reclined, where the outline of the gland is easier to follow. When the masseter and parotid are both treated, each is dosed based on its own criteria. What to watch. Dry mouth after parotid BoNT is uncommon in the authors’ experience, and the published cosmetic parotid series and trial reported no serious adverse events [ , ]. The physiological reason is that, at rest, most saliva comes from the submandibular glands, while the parotid contributes mainly stimulated flow during eating [ ]. Direct measurements of dry mouth after cosmetic parotid treatment are lacking. The doses used for

text: 4.4. Submandibular Gland: What it does. The submandibular gland lies in the submandibular triangle, below the mandibular border and in front of the mandibular angle, under the platysma [ , ]. When the gland is prominent, it blurs the line between the jaw and neck and can look like excess fat under the jaw. Reducing it sharpens that line. Who is a good candidate. Two different patients, same site. The young patient with a small mandible. When the jaw is short and the jawline is underdeveloped, a normal-sized gland sits exposed below the mandibular border. CT data confirm that many young subjects have a gland 20 mm or more below the mandibular border [ ]. Reducing the gland helps. In these patients, jawline filler is the more active option, and the two can be combined. The older patient with a ptotic gland. The gland does not grow with age; it descends. Its distance below the mandibular border increases with age, about 0.17 mm per year, while its total volume does not change [ ]. Imaging confirms that the part of the gland below the mandible grows with age while the whole gland does not [ ]. Age-related submandibular fullness is therefore ptosis, not enlargement. BoNT reduces the bulk of the exposed part. It does not lift the gland, and the patient should know this. Many patients take the submandibular gland that blurs their jawline for fat, and ask for fat reduction. On examination, the fullness is often

text: 4.4. Submandibular Gland: the gland, or the gland with fat over it. The gland is felt as a firm, separate lobule below the mandibular border. When both are present, both are treated. A practical point for the injection, not described to the authors’ knowledge. The gland is seen in the consultation with the patient upright, and what is seen there is what is treated. On the treatment bed, it can become less prominent, or disappear, once the patient lies down. Injecting with the patient as upright as possible keeps the gland where it was seen. Who needs caution. A patient with a gland that cannot be felt. Contouring treats what shows. How. A published protocol uses 20 U in 0.2 mL at five points 5 mm apart under ultrasound, with the gland diameter falling from 15 to 10 mm at 2 months [ ]; a single-point ultrasound-guided protocol uses 15 U [ ]. The authors use 10–15 U per side, 1–2 points, a high concentration, and a small volume, and do not go above this range. Ultrasound guidance is the standard precautionary approach for this gland ( ). What to watch. Dry mouth and difficulty swallowing. This is the gland that produces most resting saliva, so dry mouth is more likely than after parotid treatment; in the authors’ experience, it occurs in approximately one in ten patients and is mild and temporary. Dysphagia has followed the spread of the toxin beneath the gland ( ). If the platysma is also treated,

text: 4.5. Depressor Anguli Oris: What it does. The depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corner down. When it is strong or overactive, the corner sits low at rest, the marionette line deepens, and the lower face looks sad or tired. Removing the pull lets the elevators lift the corner. Who is a good candidate. It works best when the muscle tone is high: the corner drops when the patient says “oo”, the marionette line is deepened, or vertical or oblique lines form below the corner of the mouth. But the corner is held by the balance of elevators and depressors, so weakening the depressor raises it in most people, and the indication can be wider than these clear cases. Who needs caution. The corner of the mouth is not held down by the depressor anguli oris alone; jowl sagging and loss of volume above the corner also pull it down. A patient who expects a large lift from depressor BoNT alone needs to be told this before treatment. The change is real but modest, and it is larger when the jowl or the volume is also treated. How. The published doses are 2–4 U per side [ ]. The authors use 2–3 U per side, 1 point, at the lower lateral part of the muscle near its origin on the mandible, lateral to the vertical line of the commissure. Of the three muscles in this area—the depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, and mentalis—the depressor anguli oris is the most superficial. It can be injected superficially,

text: 4.5. Depressor Anguli Oris: raising a wheal, which keeps the toxin away from the depressor labii inferioris. What to watch. Spread into the depressor labii inferioris gives an asymmetric smile; the superficial, lateral placement above avoids this. An observation not previously reported. When the depressor is switched off, the lip elevators lose their opponent. In a patient whose nasolabial fold is made mainly by strong elevator muscles, the fold can look deeper after depressor anguli oris BoNT. To the authors’ knowledge, this has not yet been described. Such patients should be warned. Double use. Some patients have vertical lines lateral to the marionette line, near the jawline, more oblique toward the outside. The depressor anguli oris and the platysma contribute to these. Treating them is a wrinkle treatment and a contour treatment at the same time.

text: 4.6. Platysma: What it does. The platysma is a thin sheet that extends from the chest up over the jawline into the lower face, where it runs deep to the depressor anguli oris and inserts into the modiolus and the skin of the lower lip [ , ]. When it is tight, it pulls the lower face down and blurs the jawline. Relaxing it at the level of the jawline removes that pull; the jawline becomes clearer, and the lower face looks lifted. The approach is similar to the Nefertiti lift [ ]. The treatment of platysma bands in the neck is a separate indication, with different injection points, and is not covered here. Who is a good candidate. The patient must have a muscle that is pulling. In the authors’ experience, selecting patients with visible platysma pull and firm skin is what makes the jawline result reliable. Who needs caution. The patient whose jawline is blurred mainly by fat, jowl sagging, or loose skin. Relaxing the platysma will not clear it on its own. text: 4.7. Mentalis: What it does. Mentalis BoNT is often called “cobblestone chin BoNT”. For contouring, its more important effect is on chin length. An overactive mentalis pulls the soft tissue of the chin up and in. The chin looks short and pulled back, and the lower face loses its V-line. Relaxing the muscle lets the chin return to its resting length. This has been measured: after mentalis BoNT, the chin point moved downward in 10 of 11 patients [ ]. Who is a good candidate. A patient whose chin shortens or bunches on lip closure, and whose bone is adequate. The decisive question is bone versus muscle. If the vertical length of the mandible itself is short, filler is the main treatment, and the authors add mentalis BoNT when lip closure shows mentalis overactivity—which is the case in most patients with a short chin—not as a routine for every chin filler. If the patient declines filler—many do—BoNT alone still lengthens the chin, and the authors recommend at least that. If the bone is adequate and the muscle is riding over it, BoNT alone is the best treatment. Who needs caution. A patient whose mentalis is already relaxed—no shortening or bunching on lip closure. Injections placed too high reach the orbicularis oris; too lateral, the depressor labii inferioris. What to watch. In the first few days after injection, the expression can look slightly unnatural. This is uneven relaxation before the toxin has spread evenly through the muscle, and it settles within days. When it does not settle and a localized bulge appears, the cause is fibers that were missed: the treated fibers relax, and the untreated fibers contract without opposition. This “paradoxical bulging” has been described and resolves with a supplementary injection into the remaining active fibers [ ]. Covering the full thickness of the muscle at the first injection prevents it. The mentalis also supports the lower lip [ ]. Rarely, a patient reports after mentalis BoNT that the lips do not close comfortably. In the authors’ experience, this is temporary.

text: Abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin type A (BoNT-A) dosing in facial aesthetics varies across anatomical targets, formulations, and treatment indications. This structured narrative review examined published dose ranges and the potential relevance of muscle thickness, target depth, functional anatomy, and injection localization to individualized treatment planning. English-language regulatory, clinical, anatomical, ultrasound, and consensus literature available through 13 April 2026 was considered. Evidence was interpreted according to source type, distinguishing approved product-specific regimens, controlled clinical studies, observational reports, and anatomy- or expert-derived recommendations. Muscle bulk may inform masseter contouring, but the literature does not establish a validated thickness-based dosing equation applicable across facial muscles. For facial expression muscles, contraction patterns, treatment objectives, and preservation of adjacent function are central considerations. Evidence for aesthetic dosing of the temporalis and salivary glands remains limited, and glandular indications require separate assessment from skeletal muscle treatment. Anatomically informed placement has a plausible mechanistic rationale, whereas evidence that motor-zone targeting consistently reduces toxin requirements is insufficient. text: 1. Introduction: Botulinum neurotoxin type A has become the dominant neuromodulator for the treatment of dynamic rhytids, brow imbalance, lower-face depressor overactivity, platysmal banding, and masseteric hypertrophy. It is used in on-label upper-face indications such as glabellar lines, forehead lines, and lateral canthal lines, but it is also widely used off-label in the nose, upper lip, perioral region, chin, jawline, neck, and lower facial contouring [ , , , , , ]. The breadth of indications has expanded faster than the dose literature. As a result, many injectors learn conventional dosing patterns for individual regions, such as 20 units for the glabella, 20 units for the forehead when treated with the glabella, 24 units for crow’s feet, a few units for the DAO, several units for the mentalis, and larger totals for the masseter, without necessarily understanding why different muscles require such different dosing approaches [ , , , , , ]. The mechanism of BoNT-A suggests that dosing should never be treated as a purely cosmetic ritual. After binding to high-affinity receptors at the cholinergic presynaptic terminal, the toxin undergoes internalization and cleavage of soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins, functionally blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and producing a temporary chemical denervation of the target

Clinical response depends on the balance between placement precision, local concentration, injection volume, depth, tissue plane, and the arrangement of the motor endplates that are exposed to the injected toxin [ , , , ]. A muscle can therefore be undertreated because too few units were used, but it can also be undertreated because an adequate number of units was placed in the wrong plane, too far from the active motor zone, or into a compartment separated by tendon or fascial barriers [ , , , , , , ]. This mechanistic perspective is one reason the concept of “dose per muscle” is more useful than “dose per wrinkle.” A glabellar wrinkle does not behave like a crow’s feet pattern, a perioral line, or a platysmal band, because the underlying anatomy is fundamentally different. The corrugator and procerus are small but deep and intimately related to brow position. The frontalis is broad, thin, and functionally essential for brow elevation. The lateral orbicularis oculi are superficial and radially oriented, with an adjacent risk zone for unwanted diffusion into smile elevators or extraocular structures. Introduction: masseter is a thick three-dimensional masticatory muscle that is often treated not just for movement, but for bulk reduction and facial contouring [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Although most aesthetic BoNT-A targets are muscles, selected glandular structures also influence lower- and lateral-face contour. The parotid and submandibular glands are increasingly examined as BoNT targets in sialorrhea, benign glandular hypertrophy, and gland-related facial fullness. Their dosing logic is different from muscle dosing because the desired effect is reduced secretion and glandular prominence rather than weakening of contraction [ , ]. The literature also faces a definitional problem. “Dose” is often discussed as if botulinum toxin units were interchangeable between products, but they are not. The potency assays for onabotulinumtoxinA, incobotulinumtoxinA, abobotulinumtoxinA, prabotulinumtoxinA, and letibotulinumtoxinA are not standardized to a common biological unit, and the available evidence does not support a universal conversion ratio that can be safely applied across all indications [ ]. In aesthetic practice, many clinicians use pragmatic rules of thumb, but those rules do not eliminate product-specific differences in concentration, spread, reconstitution preferences, labeling history, and the way dose–response is expressed in published trials [ , , ]. Another important unresolved question is how much muscle thickness should influence dose. In routine practice, clinicians often assume that larger, stronger, or thicker muscles require more toxin. That assumption is intuitively correct in some situations, especially in masseteric hypertrophy. Yet the relationship is far less straightforward in thin facial muscles. A strong frontalis may require a conservative dose if the patient relies on it to support the brow. Thin perioral muscles may still require only small doses because their therapeutic window is narrow. A thicker corrugator can produce severe vertical glabellar lines, but inaccurate depth or excessive medial diffusion can still create ptosis even with a moderate dose [ , , , , , ]. Thickness, in other words, is not irrelevant, but it is not equivalent to safe dose capacity. In parallel with these questions, a second line of evidence has become increasingly influential: the importance of injecting close to neuromuscular junction-rich zones or intramuscular neural arborization areas. If part of the required dose is compensating for imperfect placement, then better placement may allow similar results with fewer units, fewer touch-ups, or less diffusion into adjacent muscles. The recent spread of high-resolution ultrasound in aesthetic practice has made this question clinically relevant rather than merely theoretical [ , , , , , , ]. The present review was therefore developed around four practical questions. First, what dose ranges are supported by the current literature for the major facial muscles used in cosmetic BoNT-A treatment? Second, how should these doses be interpreted across different muscles and formulations? Third, does muscle thickness correlate with dose in a clinically meaningful way? Fourth, can NMJ-targeted or distributed motor-zone injection improve efficiency enough to reduce total units? The goal is not to provide a rigid universal chart, because such a chart would ignore the variability of facial anatomy and the non-interchangeability of products. Rather, the aim is to build a structured, evidence-based dosing framework that helps the reader understand why some muscles tolerate broad dose ranges whereas others demand tiny increments and great anatomical precision. text: 1. Introduction: is safety. Most clinically significant adverse events in aesthetic BoNT-A therapy are not systemic toxicities; they are local failures of anatomy, dosing logic, or diffusion control. Eyelid ptosis, brow flattening, smile asymmetry, lip incompetence, speech alteration, dysphagia, paradoxical bulging, and impaired mastication are all examples of what can happen when a dose is selected without adequate respect for target depth, muscle function, or adjacent anatomy [ , , , , , , ]. A muscle-specific review is therefore not only about efficacy; it is also about understanding where the therapeutic window is wide, where it is narrow, and where better targeting may be more important than escalating units.

text: 2. Results: The retrieved literature does not support a single universal dosing rule across facial botulinum neurotoxin type A (BoNT-A) targets. Instead, the evidence varies according to the anatomical target, treatment indication, toxin formulation, and study design. For clinical interpretation, the targets can be organized into four indication-related groups. The first comprises established aesthetic indications involving the glabellar complex, forehead, and lateral canthal region, for which regulatory labeling and controlled clinical investigations provide relatively standardized formulation-specific treatment regimens [ , , , , , , , , ]. The second includes predominantly off-label aesthetic applications involving perinasal, perioral, selected periocular, and lower-face mimetic muscles, where anatomical investigations, expert consensus, and smaller clinical studies contribute substantially to dose selection [ , , , , , , , , , , , ]. The third encompasses facial and cervical contouring, particularly treatment of masseteric hypertrophy and platysmal prominence, for which clinical outcomes depend on both muscular activity and changes in contour or muscle volume [ , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Several anatomical and clinical principles recur across these indication groups, although the strength of supporting evidence is not uniform. First, the distribution of a formulation-specific total dose may influence treatment response through differences in target coverage, injection volume, tissue plane, and proximity to motor endplate-rich regions [ , , , , , , ]. However, anatomical plausibility and experimental evidence should not be interpreted as proof that a particular distribution strategy consistently achieves equivalent clinical efficacy with fewer units across all facial targets. Second, the functional consequences of unintended muscle weakening differ substantially by region. In the lower face, even modest off-target effects involving the depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis, or orbicularis oris may produce visible asymmetry or interfere with oral function [ , , , , ]. Consequently, conservative, indication-specific dose selection is especially important in these regions.

Nevertheless, thickness alone cannot establish an appropriate dose or replace assessment of muscle function, previous treatment, and adjacent anatomical structures [ , , , , , , , , ]. The temporalis and salivary gland literature further illustrates the importance of distinguishing treatment mechanisms and indications. The temporalis is a masticatory muscle whose size and activity may be relevant to selected functional or contour-related presentations, including compensatory recruitment after masseter treatment. By contrast, the parotid and submandibular glands are secretory structures, and their BoNT-A treatment is primarily supported by functional salivary indications and anatomical localization studies rather than by the same dose–response evidence used for facial mimetic muscles [ , , , , , ]. Gland dimensions and surrounding structures may influence localization and safety, but gland thickness should not be assumed to determine dose in the same manner as muscle hypertrophy. Accordingly, functional salivary treatment data should not be directly extrapolated to aesthetic glandular contouring. Product Non-Interchangeability as a Prerequisite for Dose Interpretation: Before considering any muscle-specific recommendations, it is necessary to restate that BoNT units are product-specific [ ]. OnabotulinumtoxinA is the most useful reference point for literature synthesis because many studies, the historic U.S. labeling pathway, and a large body of full-face practice patterns are anchored to this formulation. However, even when approximate clinical conversion customs exist, they should not be mistaken for validated equivalence across every indication or muscle. A dose of 20 units in the glabella means something very specific if it refers to onabotulinumtoxinA, but it does not become universally transferable merely because a clinician informally uses a ratio to another toxin in practice [ , , ]. Product non-interchangeability is particularly important when interpreting lower-face, cervical, masticatory, and glandular studies, because the literature includes multiple BoNT-A formulations and frequently reports different dose units, treatment patterns, and clinical endpoints [ , , , , , ]. For this reason, distinguishes doses reported in regulatory labeling and clinical investigations from the authors’ proposed clinical synthesis. text: 2.3. The Variables That Modify Dose Across All Muscles: Five interrelated factors modify dose interpretation across facial targets. First, muscle function determines the potential consequences of weakening. For example, frontalis treatment must account for its role in brow elevation, whereas lower-face depressor treatment must consider the balance between opposing muscle groups [ , , , , , , ]. Second, muscle geometry and anatomical depth influence target accessibility and treatment distribution; thin superficial muscles and bulky multilayered muscles should not be approached using identical anatomical assumptions [ , , , , , , ]. Third, baseline muscle activity, hypertrophy, and the intended outcome influence the relevance of muscle volume to dose selection. This relationship is particularly important for masseter contouring, where reduction in muscle thickness or volume is itself a treatment outcome [ , , , , , , , ]. Fourth, proximity to functionally important adjacent structures affects the consequences of toxin spread and may justify a more conservative approach in anatomically sensitive regions [ , , , , , ]. Fifth, previous BoNT-A exposure and treatment response may influence subsequent dosing. Repeated treatment of hypertrophic masticatory muscles may produce persistent changes in muscle thickness or volume, so maintenance doses should not automatically reproduce initial doses without reassessment. A sixth consideration is whether imaging can provide clinically useful information beyond conventional anatomical and functional assessment. Ultrasound can visualize variation in muscle thickness, depth, and topography, including differences between individuals and between sides of the same face [ , , , , , ]. Nevertheless, ultrasound should be regarded as a selective adjunct rather than a universal requirement for facial BoNT-A treatment. Established superficial aesthetic indications can generally be assessed using clinical examination, dynamic facial movement, and anatomical landmarks. Imaging may offer additional value in patients with marked asymmetry, previous treatment-related anatomical changes, uncertain target localization, substantial muscle hypertrophy, or complex glandular anatomy. For repeated masseter or temporalis treatment, ultrasound may help document changes in thickness and guide reassessment of treatment strategy, although thickness measurements alone do not define a validated dose-adjustment algorithm [ , , , , , , , ]. text: 2.4. Why Is the Evidence Stronger for Some Muscles than for Others: The certainty with which dose ranges can be interpreted differs substantially among anatomical targets. For established upper-face indications, regulatory labeling and controlled clinical trials provide formulation-specific dosing frameworks, although these frameworks do not necessarily establish the optimal dose for every constituent muscle or individual patient [ , , , , , , , , ]. For masseter treatment, prospective investigations, randomized studies, and ultrasound-based assessments contribute evidence regarding muscular and contour-related outcomes, but differences in formulation, baseline hypertrophy, outcome measures, and follow-up limit direct comparisons [ , , , , , , , ]. Platysmal treatment is supported by anatomical investigations and controlled clinical trial evidence, including phase 3 evaluation of onabotulinumtoxinA [ , , ]. In contrast, many perinasal, perioral, and lower-face applications remain dependent on smaller studies, anatomical rationale, and expert consensus, making precise dose–response conclusions less certain [ , , , , , , , , , , ]. The existence of a commonly used clinical dose should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the dose has been validated in a randomized trial.
