Inflammatory and Oxidative Stress Pathways Psychological stress not only affects immune balance, but it also initiates chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative damage in the skin. Studies have shown that stress increases circulating levels of inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and prostaglandins, all of which contribute to microinflammation around the hair follicle [ ]. This environment disrupts the function of key follicular structures such as the dermal papilla and arrector pili muscle, pushing hair prematurely from the anagen (growth) phase into the telogen (shedding) phase. Prie al. [ ] further demonstrated that oxidative stress exacerbated by chronic psychological load can impair mitochondrial function in follicular cells, accelerating their entry into the catagen phase and leading to miniaturization of hair shafts. Supporting this, Du et al. [ ] have highlighted how oxidative stress modulates key pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), and TGF-β, thereby altering the homeostasis and regeneration of hair follicles. Neurobiology of Trichotillomania (TTM) and Compulsive Behaviors TTM is more than a behavioral compulsion; it is a psychiatric disorder rooted in neurobiological dysfunction, particularly in the circuits responsible for impulse regulation and habit formation. Neuroimaging research has consistently revealed abnormalities in the anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal striatum, and related frontostriatal pathways regions integral to monitoring behavior, suppressing urges, and modulating emotional responses [ , ]. Dysregulation in these areas may impair top-down control over motor actions, making individuals more susceptible to the involuntary, repetitive hair-pulling that characterizes TTM. Additionally, disruptions in neurotransmitter systems, especially involving serotonin and dopamine, likely contribute to the rewarding or tension-relieving sensations reported by patients following hair-pulling episodes, reinforcing the compulsive behavior through maladaptive reward processing. In some cases, these neurochemical and circuit-based disturbances overlap with those observed in obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorders, supporting the idea of shared mechanistic pathways [ ]. Depression, Anxiety, and BDNF-Linked Hair Loss Depression and anxiety frequently coexist with hair loss, especially in cases of TE and androgenetic alopecia. These associations are not purely circumstantial; they are supported by shared neurobiological pathways. Chronic stress and mood disorders are known to lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein involved in both emotional resilience and follicular health [ , ]. Reduced BDNF impairs the activity of dermal papilla cells, disrupts hair cycling, and contributes to follicular miniaturization. This connection suggests that strategies aimed at restoring BDNF through antidepressants, exercise, stress-reduction techniques, or certain nutritional supplements may benefit both psychological well-being and hair growth. Dai et al. [ ] found that lifestyle interventions targeting BDNF levels were linked to improvements in both mood and follicular integrity. Studies have shown a gradual decline in stem cell renewal within hair follicles, reduced blood supply to the scalp, and lower levels of essential growth factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) [ , ]. These changes collectively shorten the hair growth phase and produce finer, less dense hair over time. While sometimes dismissed as a normal part of aging, this form of hair loss can still take a psychological toll. Older adults may feel less confident, avoid social situations, or struggle with body image, especially in societies that closely tie youth and appearance. In patients already coping with age-related transitions or emotional stressors, hair loss may further contribute to anxiety or depressive symptoms [ , ]. Somatic Symptom Disorder (SSD) and Subjective Hair Complaints In some patients, complaints of hair loss occur despite normal clinical findings. This is often seen in individuals with SSD, where physical symptoms are driven by emotional distress rather than objective pathology. Patients may report increased shedding, fragility, or thinning, even though scalp examination reveals no signs of active alopecia. Cultural Variability in Hair Loss Perception The psychological response to hair loss is shaped not only by individual personality but also by cultural beliefs about appearance, aging, and gender. In many Western societies, a full head of hair is often associated with attractiveness, vitality, and social status. As a result, individuals experiencing hair thinning or baldness may internalize feelings of inadequacy or face stigma, especially women, who are more likely to experience social judgment tied to physical appearance [ ]. However, this is not universal. In some cultures, hair loss is normalized or even respected, viewed as a natural part of aging or a symbol of wisdom. These variations influence how individuals interpret their condition and how likely they are to seek treatment or report emotional distress. Recognizing these cultural differences allows clinicians to provide more personalized, empathetic care and helps ensure that patient expectations and concerns are addressed in a way that feels relevant and respectful [ ]. Table summarizes the major biological and psychological mechanisms discussed, offering a visual model of how chronic stress may drive follicular damage across various forms of alopecia. Understanding the intersection between psychiatric health and dermatological conditions, particularly hair loss, has become an increasingly important focus in clinical research. Often dismissed as a cosmetic concern, hair loss can have profound psychological consequences, triggering or worsening conditions such as anxiety, depression, and BDD. Psychiatric illness can, in turn, provoke or exacerbate hair loss through behavioral, neuroendocrine, and immunological mechanisms. This literature review reveals a complex, bidirectional relationship between mental health and hair disorders, reinforcing the importance of integrative, multidisciplinary care models. The following discussion synthesizes the physiological and psychological findings and explores their implications for clinical practice. These mechanisms collectively illustrate how psychological distress can provoke autoimmune hair loss. From a clinical standpoint, this reinforces the importance of considering both emotional health and immune function in the management of alopecia areata. Treatment plans that integrate psychological support alongside immunotherapies may improve outcomes by addressing both the physical and emotional components of disease activity. Interventions aimed at restoring neuroendocrine balance, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, regular exercise, and sleep optimization, have demonstrated potential in reversing these effects [ , ]. As this field evolves, its integration into psychodermatologic practice may pave the way for more precise and holistic treatment strategies. From a clinical perspective, successful management of TTM and related disorders requires a multidisciplinary approach. BDNF deficiency impairs dermal papilla cell function and hinders follicular regeneration. Therefore, interventions that enhance BDNF levels, whether pharmacologic, psychotherapeutic, or lifestyle-based, may offer dual benefits for both psychological and dermatologic outcomes [ ]. Clinically, this underscores the value of holistic treatment models that integrate psychiatric care with dermatologic support, addressing the full scope of patient needs. Age-related hair loss, or senescent alopecia, introduces additional biological and psychological considerations. Unlike androgenetic alopecia, senescent alopecia is characterized by diffuse thinning without a distinct pattern and occurs independently of androgenic activity, typically manifesting after the age of 50. Mechanistically, it is associated with decreased follicular stem cell activity, reduced vascular supply, and a decline in growth factors such as IGF-1 and VEGF [ , ]. From a psychosocial perspective, older adults may experience lowered self-esteem or social withdrawal in response to progressive hair thinning, especially in societies that equate youth with beauty and vitality [ , ]. Stress-induced dysbiosis impairs gut integrity, promoting systemic inflammation and altering hormonal signaling pathways, which can negatively affect both mood and scalp health [ , ]. Preliminary findings suggest that probiotics and dietary modification may offer dual benefits, supporting microbiome balance and reducing stress-related hair shedding [ ]. Although clinical evidence is still developing, this pathway offers promising insight into how internal stress responses can manifest externally, reinforcing the need for integrative approaches in psychodermatologic care. Psychiatric treatment itself may sometimes become a contributing factor to hair loss. SSRIs, lithium, and valproate are known to disrupt hair cycling, with reported TE rates between 9% and 16% [ , ]. These agents may prematurely terminate the anagen phase or impact follicular metabolism. Zhang et al. [ ] emphasized that individual genetic variation can further influence susceptibility. These findings underline the importance of early identification and open communication. When patients are informed of potential side effects and supported in adjusting their treatment plan,

SSD adds a unique layer of diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in cases of unexplained hair loss. These individuals often report significant distress and preoccupation with perceived hair changes despite objective dermatologic normalcy. Emerging evidence suggests that dysregulation of the HPA axis, particularly sustained elevations in cortisol, may contribute to heightened somatic focus and emotional amplification [ , ]. Functional neuroimaging studies have also implicated aberrant activity in regions governing emotional salience and interoceptive processing, such as the anterior insula and amygdala. Clinically, simple reassurance tends to fall short. Instead, effective management typically requires an integrated approach involving psychiatric consultation, cognitive-behavioral strategies, and psychoeducation to address the underlying affective drivers and reduce the risk of chronic disability. This mind-body connection was further illuminated during the COVID-19 pandemic, which brought both biological and psychological stressors to the forefront. SARS-CoV-2 infection triggered immune dysregulation, while the psychological toll of grief, isolation, and fear activated the HPA axis, contributing to widespread cases of TE [ , ]. Addressing the emotional impact alongside physical symptoms can help patients better understand the temporary nature of the condition and improve adherence to treatment and follow-up. Psychological stress is increasingly recognized as a key factor in the pathogenesis of various hair disorders. Research shows that stress-induced oxidative damage and inflammatory cytokine activity can disrupt hair follicle cycling and mitochondrial function, leading to early follicle regression and shedding [ ]. While much of this evidence comes from Western cohorts, emerging data from developing countries also highlight similar trends under different societal stressors. For instance, a multicenter study conducted in Saudi Arabia found that patients with alopecia areata experienced significant psychological impacts, including anxiety and depression, underscoring the need for comprehensive care approaches that address both dermatological and psychological aspects of the condition [ ]. Similarly, research from Nepal reported high prevalence rates of depression and anxiety among alopecia areata patients, emphasizing the psychological burden of the disease in diverse cultural contexts [ ]. These culturally embedded narratives influence not only the degree of psychological distress but also the likelihood of seeking treatment. Clinicians who remain attuned to such cultural dimensions are better equipped to deliver care that is both empathetic and contextually appropriate, fostering more meaningful communication and alignment with patient expectations [ , ]. This review brings together a broad and interdisciplinary range of perspectives to better understand the connection between psychiatric disorders and hair loss. One of its key strengths is the way it integrates research across dermatology, psychiatry, immunology, and neurobiology fields that are often considered separately in clinical practice. By bridging these disciplines, the review sheds light on both the emotional and biological drivers behind hair loss, including immune system shifts, hormonal changes, neurotrophic factors, and gut-brain interactions. Another strength lies in the study’s focus on recent literature, capturing up-to-date findings that reflect emerging patterns in patient care and scientific understanding. text: Abstract: Telogen effluvium post-COVID-19 is a condition characterized by the diffuse and reversible loss of scalp hair in the period following infection with SARS-CoV-2, and it is currently the second cause of alopecia in women. In the context of the COVID-19 infection, intense psychological stress contributes to alopecia appearance, along with systemic inflammation, autoimmune reactions, oxidative stress, and virally induced hypoxia. Cytokines with proinflammatory action and vasoactive substances negatively modulate the metabolism of some molecules, such as proteoglycans, involved in the hair follicle’s growth cycle. Studies show that a large percentage of hairs will suddenly enter the catagen phase during a moderate to severe COVID-19 infection. In the present paper, we update the data from the literature with a clinical example. Our case highlighted that the telogen effluvium after infections with SARS-CoV-2 is reversible with appropriate dermatological treatment. For therapeutic success, informing the patient about this pathology’s self-limited and reversible character is essential to reduce the emotional stress that may aggravate the disease.

To establish the diagnosis, it is essential to perform a detailed anamnesis that highlights the excessive and diffuse hair loss in the post-infection period with SARS-CoV-2, which must be corroborated with the dermatological and trichoscopic examination. Trichoscopy reveals the diffuse reduction of hair density, short hairs, and multiple bare follicles in places, which present aspects similar to the classic forms of TE [ ]. Considering the predominance of the condition in women, we can consider that estrogens and progesterone may be involved in the pathogenesis of telogen effluvium. Their effects are immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory, thus protecting the hair follicle. Estradiol alters the hair follicle growth and cycle through its receptors. Progesterone decreases the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, with effects on the hair cycle, thereby shortening the anagen phase. Thus, hair loss in women infected with COVID-19 may be due to the viral infection causing a significant reduction in systemic estrogen and progesterone levels [ ]. In a viral context, SARS-CoV-2 increases the level of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL6—interleukin 6, TNFα—tumor necrosis factor α, and IL1β—interleukin 1β), decreases various growth factors (IGF1—insulin-like growth factor 1, TGF β1—transforming growth factor β1, VEGF—vascular endothelial growth factor, and FGF β—fibroblastic growth factor β), with the result being the apoptosis of follicular keratinocytes. The causes and mechanisms of hair loss are multifaceted, including genetics, hormone levels, immune regulation, cytokines, growth factors, stress, and other factors. The main types of hair loss include androgenetic alopecia, alopecia areata, and chemotherapy-induced hair loss. Treatments for hair loss are also continuously advancing, including pharmaceutical treatments, adipose-derived stem cells (Fig. a) and their derivatives, and the application of traditional Chinese medicine and its active ingredients [ ]. Androgenetic Alopecia (AGA) is the most common type of hair loss, and its pathogenesis may be influenced by the interaction of multiple genetic and environmental factors [ ]. The development of AGA is closely associated with the role of androgens (Fig. c), particularly dihydrotestosterone (DHT) [ ]. DHT binds to androgen receptors in the hair follicles, causing them to shrink gradually, shortening the anagen phase, and ultimately leading to hair thinning and shedding [ ]. AGA manifests differently in males and females [ ]. In males, AGA typically presents as hair loss at the forehead and crown areas, while in females, it appears as diffuse thinning on the top of the scalp. This gender difference may be related to the expression levels of androgen receptors and associated enzymes in the hair follicles [ ]. text: Telogen Effluvium: Telogen Effluvium (TE) is a common type of hair loss characterized by the sudden shedding of a large number of hairs that are typically in the telogen (resting) phase [ ]. This type of hair loss can be acute or chronic and is typically associated with external factors such as physiological or psychological stress, malnutrition, illness, medication side effects, and hormonal changes [ ]. The diagnosis of TE primarily relies on patient history and clinical presentation, and sometimes, a scalp biopsy is necessary to rule out other types of hair loss [ ]. Acute Telogen Effluvium (TE) typically occurs within 3–4 months after a triggering event, presenting as diffuse hair loss, and the hair can fully regrow within several months after the removal of the trigger [ ]. Chronic TE, on the other hand, manifests as persistent, unexplained hair loss, and recovery may take longer. The key to treating TE is identifying and removing the trigger; medications such as corticosteroids and minoxidil can also be used for treatment [ ]. TE differs from other types of hair loss, such as Androgenetic Alopecia (AGA) and Alopecia Areata. AGA usually presents with a specific pattern of hair loss, while Alopecia Areata results in patchy hair loss. TE typically causes diffuse shedding; on dermoscopy, an increase in vellus hairs and a reduction in pigmentation can be observed [ ]. In terms of treatment,

text: Alopecia Areata: Alopecia Areata (AA) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the appearance of round or oval-shaped hair loss patches on the scalp or other areas of the body [ ]. The exact pathogenesis of this disease is not yet fully understood, but it is closely related to genetic and environmental factors. The pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, and treatment progress of Alopecia Areata can be explored from several perspectives. The pathogenesis of Alopecia Areata involves multiple factors, including genetics, immune system abnormalities, and environmental factors. Genetic factors play an essential role in the development of AA. Studies show that some patients with Alopecia Areata have a family history, indicating that genetics contribute significantly to its occurrence. Additionally, abnormal immune responses are a key mechanism in the development of AA. Alopecia Areata is considered an autoimmune disease, where the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, causing them to enter the telogen phase and resulting in hair loss [ ]. In particular, CD8+ NKG2D+ T cells dominate follicular pathology, although the exact mechanism remains unclear [ ].

text: Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis: The clinical presentation of Alopecia Areata varies, ranging from a single hair loss patch to total hair loss on the body [ ]. Most patients develop symptoms before the age of 30, and the clinical types of AA include patchy, reticulate, and diffuse forms. The diagnosis of Alopecia Areata is typically based on clinical signs, such as non-scarring, round hair loss patches, and the early-stage “exclamation mark” hairs [ ]. In more complex or unusual cases, biopsy and histological examination may be used to assist in the diagnosis.

text: Treatment Progress: Although Alopecia Areata has no cure, treatment methods have progressed [ ]. Traditional treatments include topical or systemic corticosteroids, local immunotherapy, and topical hair growth stimulants [ ]. In recent years, new immunotherapy drugs, such as small molecule drugs and biologics, have also shown promise [ ]. However, the effectiveness of these treatments is inconsistent, and treatment interruptions often lead to relapse of Alopecia Areata. Alopecia Areata is a complex autoimmune disease with pathogenesis involving genetics, immune system abnormalities, and environmental factors. Despite some progress in current treatments, many challenges remain, such as the inconsistency in treatment outcomes and high relapse rates. Future research needs to clarify the specific mechanisms of Alopecia Areata further to develop more effective and safer treatment options.

text: Unresolved Controversies and Debates in Hair Loss Pathophysiology: Multiple pieces of evidence indicate the presence of “microinflammation” around hair follicles in AGA patients, manifested as infiltration of lymphocytes and mast cells, and elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, TGF-β1) [ , ]. This inflammation may be triggered by metabolic products of scalp microbiota (such as Propionibacterium acnes ) or oxidative stress, leading to follicular fibrosis and thickening of the collagen sheath, which accelerates follicular miniaturization [ , ]. Additionally, androgens may directly induce inflammation by activating innate immune responses (such as the TLR pathway) [ ]. Some studies suggest that inflammation is a consequence rather than a cause of follicular degeneration. For example, R. English et al. point out that the heterogeneity of biopsy sites and hair follicle miniaturization stages (HFM) may lead to biases in inflammation detection results and the degree of inflammation may not be directly correlated with hair loss progression [ ]. Furthermore, although finasteride inhibits DHT production, it does not significantly improve inflammatory markers, suggesting that inflammation may be a secondary event [ , ]. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationship between inflammation and AGA, and single-cell transcriptomics should be used to analyze the subtypes of inflammatory cells and signaling pathways [ , ].

In addition, the causes of hair loss include immune dysfunction, skin diseases, environmental factors, nutrition-related hair loss, and medication-induced hair loss [ ]. text: Environmental Factors: Environmental factors have a multifaceted impact on the scalp and hair follicles, including air pollution, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, and chemical exposure. These factors influence hair health and growth through various mechanisms [ ]. Air pollution, especially particulate matter (such as PM10), has been shown to reduce the levels of proteins that promote hair growth on the scalp, thus promoting hair loss (Fig. b) [ ]. In addition, airborne pollutants such as tobacco smoke and phthalates, which are endocrine disruptors, may also indirectly affect the function of hair follicles [ ]. UV radiation is another significant environmental factor that affects hair follicles’ physical structure and physiological functions and induces oxidative stress and changes in the micro-ecology, leading to inflammation around the hair follicles. UV exposure can also cause hair follicle stem cells and dermal papilla cells to age, further promoting hair loss [ ]. Exposure to chemicals, such as ingredients in hair dyes and styling products, is another important factor leading to hair damage [ ]. These chemicals can damage the structure and function of hair, making it brittle, prone to breakage, or causing hair loss [ ]. For instance, the chemicals in hair dyes can cause melanin deposition in the cuticle and cortex, which provides some protection against UV light but may negatively affect hair health

text: Abstract: Alopecia has recently been reported as a potential emerging adverse effect associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), which are widely prescribed for weight loss. While gastrointestinal symptoms remain the most frequently documented adverse effects, an increasing number of reports describe hair loss events in patients treated with semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide, and dulaglutide. This scoping review aimed to synthesize the available evidence regarding this potential association. A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, Cochrane, and the Latin American and Caribbean Literature on Health Sciences (LILACS) database through May 24, 2025. Nine studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized clinical trials, cohort studies, and pharmacovigilance analyses. Most studies lacked dermatological diagnostic confirmation, and only one described the clinical pattern of alopecia, identifying telogen effluvium and androgenetic alopecia as the most frequent subtypes. The findings suggest that GLP-1RAs may alter the hair follicle cycle. These agents, such as semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide, were initially developed for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, but have demonstrated significant clinical benefits in achieving sustained weight loss, leading to their approval for obesity management even in individuals without diabetes [ ]. The most commonly reported adverse effects in clinical trials and post-marketing surveillance include gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation [ ]. However, alopecia has been noted in cohort studies with limited sample sizes [ , ] and pharmacovigilance analyses [ ], with no comprehensive clinical characterization currently available to determine its prevalence, clinical features, or underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Although infrequent, this adverse effect raises concern due to its potential impact on treatment adherence and patient quality of life. The available studies vary widely in design, quality, populations, and reporting of alopecia outcomes, which precludes conducting a quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis. However, the lack of data on event timing, alopecia subtype, patient history, and outcomes following drug discontinuation limits the analysis and leaves key questions unanswered for future investigation. In this context, we propose an integrative pathophysiological hypothesis to explain alopecia in patients using GLP-1RAs. Rapid weight loss induced by these agents generates acute metabolic stress, which may trigger telogen effluvium, a transient, non-scarring form of hair loss well documented in the context of bariatric surgery, systemic illness, or strict hypocaloric diets [ , ]. Additionally, some studies suggest that these agents could also act as triggers for androgenetic alopecia in predisposed individuals, partly through hormonal modulation during weight loss [ ]. More speculatively, indirect mechanisms have been proposed involving the expression of GLP-1 receptors in dermal fibroblasts and adipose-derived stem cells. This review highlights the urgent need for systematic clinical research that includes alopecia as a safety endpoint in prospective trials. Standardized dermatologic evaluations should be incorporated, including targeted medical history, trichoscopy, clinical classification of alopecia subtypes, and scalp biopsy when indicated, along with structured longitudinal monitoring. It is also crucial to improve pharmacovigilance systems to enhance the detection and clinical characterization of dermatologic adverse events with greater precision.

text: Conclusions: Alopecia has been repeatedly reported as a potential emerging and undercharacterized adverse effect in patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists prescribed for weight loss. While the available evidence is limited and heterogeneous, the recurrence of cases across different clinical contexts suggests a relevant safety signal that deserves attention. Although a conclusive causal relationship cannot be established, the association carries meaningful clinical implications, particularly concerning treatment adherence and quality of life. This review offers a first comprehensive mapping of the existing literature and underscores the need for future investigations incorporating systematic dermatologic characterization, precise temporal assessment, and longitudinal follow-up. Furthermore, the proposed pathophysiological hypothesis opens a novel line of research into the metabolic, hormonal, and dermatologic impact of these agents, contributing to a more holistic understanding of their effects beyond weight control.

text: Abstract: Background and Objectives : Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a complex pathophysiology that continues to challenge effective long-term disease management. Hippophae rhamnoides (sea buckthorn) is a phytochemically rich medicinal plant with reported anti-inflammatory and dermo-reparative properties. Materials and Methods : A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines using the PubMed database. text: 1. Introduction: Sea buckthorn (SB), also known as Hippophae rhamnoides , is a deciduous shrub rich in nutrients belonging to the family Elaeagnaceae , mostly found in coastal areas, river banks and mountainous zones in Eastern Europe and Asia [ ]. SB has a long history as a therapeutic substance, being used to treat different skin-associated health problems (it was used for skin repair, UV-photoprotection, in psoriasis, allergic and atopic dermatitis, acne, ichthyosis) for thousands of years in several different cultures [ , , ]. This paper examines the therapeutic potential of the phytochemical profile by relating it to the principal pathophysiological pathways implicated in inflammatory dermatological disorders. The biological effects of SB are mediated by modulating key molecular pathways: suppression of inflammation via down-regulation of NF-κB signaling, attenuation of oxidative stress through activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, and improvement of endothelial function by enhancing nitric oxide bioavailability. Its bioactive compounds (flavonoids, carotenoids, and unsaturated fatty acids) also contribute to immune regulation and protection against vascular dysfunction associated with chronic inflammation and oxidative stress [ , ]. The antioxidant composition differs between plant parts, contributing to the species’ documented biological, physiological, and medicinal benefits [ , ].

text: 3.2. Inflammatory Cutaneous Pathophysiology of Rosacea: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder with a multifactorial and highly complex pathophysiology, in which molecular dysregulation of innate immunity, neurovascular signaling, and microbial interactions plays a central role. At the molecular level, increased expression and activation of Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) in keratinocytes have been identified as key initiating events, leading to enhanced production and abnormal proteolytic processing of the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin into proinflammatory fragments. These cathelicidin-derived peptides promote leukocyte chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix degradation, thereby sustaining cutaneous inflammation and vascular remodeling characteristic of rosacea [ , ]. Concomitantly, upregulation of serine proteases, such as kallikrein 5, further amplifies inflammatory cascades and contributes to epidermal barrier dysfunction [ ]. Neurovascular dysregulation represents an additional molecular axis in rosacea pathogenesis, involving altered expression of transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels, including TRPV1 and TRPA1, on sensory nerves and keratinocytes. Activation of these channels by environmental triggers induces the release of vasoactive neuropeptides, such as substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide, which drive vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and neurogenic inflammation [ ,

Microbial factors further modulate molecular inflammatory pathways in rosacea. Increased density of Demodex mites has been associated with enhanced expression of inflammatory mediators, including matrix metalloproteinases and reactive oxygen species, which exacerbate tissue damage and vascular changes [ , ]. The presence of Demodex folliculorum in increased numbers within follicular openings in rosacea induces these changes, both directly and indirectly through its endosymbionts, and may also be involved in the ocular form of rosacea [ , , ]. In parallel, alterations in the cutaneous and intestinal microbiome may influence systemic and local immune signaling, promoting chronic inflammation through cytokine-mediated pathways and reinforcing the concept of a gut–skin axis in rosacea [ , ]. Collectively, these molecular insights underscore rosacea as a disease driven by interconnected immunologic, neurovascular, and microbial signaling networks, providing a rationale for the development of targeted molecular therapies aimed at interrupting specific pathogenic pathways [ , ] ( ).

Discussion: This review synthesizes recent evidence regarding the dermatological and anti-inflammatory potential of Hippophae rhamnoides , with a particular focus on mechanisms relevant to rosacea and related inflammatory skin disorders. The studies summarized in collectively reveal several consistent mechanistic patterns that support the biological plausibility of sea buckthorn-based interventions in chronic cutaneous inflammation. A dominant and recurring theme across the included studies is the central role of inflammatory signaling pathways regulated by nuclear factor kappa B. Multiple experimental investigations demonstrate that both whole extracts and isolated compounds derived from Hippophae rhamnoides suppress nuclear factor kappa B activation, leading to reduced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and mediators [ , , , ]. This mechanism is consistently observed across diverse biological systems, including keratinocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, mast cells, and epithelial barrier models. Importantly, one of the studies directly addressing rosacea shows that quercetin interacts with key regulators of nuclear factor kappa B signaling, resulting in attenuation of immune infiltration and vascular dysfunction [ ]. The convergence of these findings across different disease models suggests that modulation of nuclear factor kappa B signaling represents a core anti-inflammatory

From a translational perspective, future research should follow a stepwise strategy. Large scale and rigorously designed in vivo studies should be prioritized to confirm efficacy, safety, and dose–response relationships under standardized conditions. These studies should subsequently be complemented by mechanistic in vitro investigations aimed at validating molecular targets, clarifying signaling pathways, and identifying potential synergistic interactions between different classes of bioactive compounds. Only if preclinical findings remain robust and reproducible should progression toward human studies be considered. At that stage, carefully designed clinical trials with clearly defined endpoints, adequate sample sizes, and disease-specific stratification will be essential. Clinical Implications and Limitations: Despite the promising biological effects observed in experimental models, the current body of evidence does not support the clinical use of Hippophae rhamnoides as a standalone therapeutic intervention for the treatment of rosacea or other inflammatory skin diseases. As summarized in , the majority of studies are conducted at a preclinical or early translational level and do not meet the criteria required for routine clinical application. At present, the absence of standardized formulations, limited large-scale in vivo validation, and lack of robust rosacea-specific clinical trials represent major barriers to clinical translation. Furthermore, variability in extract composition and dosing raises concerns regarding reproducibility, safety, and interindividual variability in therapeutic response. These limitations highlight the risks associated with premature clinical adoption. From a clinical standpoint, Hippophae rhamnoides should therefore be regarded as an experimental or investigational candidate rather than an established therapeutic option. Current findings are valuable for hypothesis generation and future trial design, but they are insufficient to inform clinical decision-making. text: 5. Conclusions: This review integrates recent experimental and translational findings examining the dermatological and anti-inflammatory properties of Hippophae rhamnoides . As summarized in , available studies suggest that sea buckthorn derived compounds can influence several biological processes implicated in inflammatory skin disorders, including immune signaling, oxidative stress responses, vascular regulation, and epithelial barrier function. A consistent observation across experimental models is the modulation of inflammatory and barrier-related pathways by sea buckthorn constituents. Multiple studies report reductions in pro-inflammatory mediators, partial restoration of barrier integrity, and attenuation of vascular or immune activation. These recurring mechanistic patterns provide a plausible biological basis for the reported effects in preclinical models, including those with relevance to rosacea-associated pathology. Nevertheless, the current evidence base is predominantly preclinical and methodologically heterogeneous. Substantial variability in extract composition, dosing regimens, experimental systems, and outcome measures limits comparability across studies and constrains the strength of translational inferences. text: Abstract: Abstract Inflammatory memory refers to functional changes retained by a tissue after an inflammatory episode that allow faster or stronger responses to subsequent challenges. It encompasses epigenetic memory in epithelial and stem cells, trained immunity, and tissue-resident memory T cells. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent flushing, persistent erythema, and papulopustular lesions, and relapse after treatment cessation is common; the mechanisms that drive recurrence remain unclear. In this hypothesis-generating critical review, we use inflammatory memory as an integrative framework and examine evidence consistent with inflammatory memory in rosacea, including the Toll-like receptor 2/kallikrein-related peptidase 5/cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (LL-37) positive feedback axis, mast-cell-mediated amplification, neuroimmune amplification, and an interleukin-1β-centered persistent inflammatory program. We draw on mechanistic evidence from psoriasis and atopic dermatitis related to tissue-resident memory T cells, epithelial memory, and trained immunity, while explicitly separating established rosacea-specific observations from indirect cross-disease parallels and speculative claims. A multilayer memory network model is proposed in which repeated triggers write memory and lower the relapse threshold; disease modification is then discussed

text: Introduction: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by centrofacial flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, and papulopustular lesions. Patients experience repeated episodes, and relapse after treatment cessation often occurs within weeks to months. In a phase III randomized controlled trial (RCT), patients with papulopustular rosacea who had responded to 16 weeks of treatment were followed after withdrawal; the median time to relapse was 115 days with ivermectin 1% cream and 85 days with metronidazole 0.75% cream ( ). In a retrospective comparative study, the 24-week no-relapse rate was 48.6% when oral metronidazole was added to oral minocycline, compared with 18.1% with minocycline alone ( ). Relapse also remains difficult to prevent even during maintenance therapy: the relapse rate during 40 weeks of maintenance with subantibiotic-dose doxycycline (40 mg once daily) was 13.8%, significantly lower than the 27.7% in the control group ( ); after treatment with 540 nm intense pulsed light, the recurrence rate at 2 years of follow-up was 8.41%, compared with 48.33% without long-term intervention ( ). Current guidelines recommend phenotype-based symptomatic treatment ( ), but available therapies mainly control active inflammation, and no disease-modifying approach exists. text: Introduction: and emotional stress, can repeatedly induce episodes, and some patients become increasingly sensitive to stimulation over time. This pattern suggests that rosacea-affected skin does not return completely to a resting state but instead retains an inflammatory condition shaped by prior episodes. Concepts such as trained immunity, epithelial inflammatory memory, and tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM) offer a framework for understanding recurrence in chronic inflammatory skin diseases. In this review, we use this framework to integrate the evidence on chronic relapse in rosacea and to discuss disease modification as a candidate therapeutic goal. Throughout the review, we distinguish three evidence levels: established rosacea-specific observations, indirect evidence from other diseases or models, and speculative hypotheses that require direct testing. We also explicitly discuss alternative explanations and contradictory findings and state what evidence would falsify the proposed model.

text: Inflammatory memory: conceptual framework and evidence boundaries: Inflammatory memory is a functional concept: after an inflammatory episode, a tissue does not return fully to baseline and instead responds faster or more strongly to subsequent stimulation. Based on the cell types that carry the memory, we classify inflammatory memory into three categories: trained immunity, epithelial/non-immune cell inflammatory memory, and TRM. Trained immunity refers to the nonspecific enhancement of responsiveness that innate immune cells, such as monocytes and macrophages, acquire after an initial stimulus. The concept was first systematically described in infection immunology, and its core mechanisms are epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming ( , ). Epigenetic changes include histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac). Training does not always have harmful consequences: macrophages trained with low-dose lipopolysaccharide (LPS) attenuated systemic sclerosis-like fibrosis, whereas macrophages trained with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) worsened fibrosis, and adoptive transfer reproduced the corresponding effects ( ). Thus, the direction and intensity of training determine its pathological outcome. Epithelial/non-immune cell inflammatory memory refers to the ability of structural cells to retain the effects of prior inflammation. text: Inflammatory memory: conceptual framework and evidence boundaries: nasal epithelial progenitor cells exposed to allergic inflammation, specifically interleukin-4 (IL-4)/interleukin-13 (IL-13), retained transcriptional memory. In one patient with concomitant severe atopic dermatitis (AD), treatment with an anti-interleukin-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα) antibody partially reset the basal cell state of nasal polyps ( ). In mouse epidermal stem cells, inflammatory memory is acquired in a stimulus-specific manner and is established by the coordinated action of the broadly acting stress-responsive transcription factors FOS and JUN together with signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). During establishment, these factors open the chromatin of memory domains; during maintenance, stem-cell transcription factors and histone-modifying enzymes keep the domains accessible. On secondary stimulation, such as full-thickness wounding, FOS rapidly re-enters memory domains and reactivates transcription, suggesting a role for this memory in tissue repair ( ). Fibroblast-like synoviocytes from patients with rheumatoid arthritis retain gene-specific chromatin-level memory after tumor necrosis factor (TNF) withdrawal and can amplify interferon responses ( ). text: Inflammatory memory: conceptual framework and evidence boundaries: long periods ( ). Clinically resolved psoriatic lesions retain CD49a + /CD103 + epidermal CD8 + TRM and type 22 helper T (Th22)/type 17 cytotoxic T (Tc17) cells that can still secrete interleukin-17 (IL-17)/interleukin-22 (IL-22) 6 years after treatment cessation ( ). Resolved lesions also contain oligoclonally expanded pathogenic IL-17 + αβ T cells ( ). The IL-17A-dominated tissue response elicited by activation of these resident T cells can stratify the risk of relapse after withdrawal of ultraviolet phototherapy ( ). In chronic skin diseases, these three categories of memory have increasingly been integrated into a unified framework of inflammatory memory ( ). The evidence above comes mainly from infection immunology, tissue repair, psoriasis, AD, airway disease, and rheumatoid arthritis; no direct molecular evidence for the three inflammatory memory layers in rosacea exists. These mechanisms can therefore serve only as analogies for generating testable hypotheses and cannot be taken as evidence that the same mechanisms operate in rosacea. To avoid overstating the strength of the current literature, we classify each claim as established, indirect, or speculative. Established claims are supported by rosacea-specific primary data, including randomized clinical trials (RCTs), cohorts, human tissue analyses, or functional experiments in relevant rosacea models. text: Evidence consistent with inflammatory memory in rosacea: Although direct molecular evidence of inflammatory memory in rosacea is lacking, several clinical and mechanistic features are consistent with memory-like behavior: a self-sustaining inflammatory axis, a stereotyped time course of relapse after treatment withdrawal, and a re-primable state in non-lesional skin. The candidate mechanism closest to inflammatory memory in rosacea is a self-sustaining positive feedback axis. The axis begins with Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2): TLR2 expression is markedly increased in the epidermis of rosacea but not in AD or psoriasis, and keratinocyte TLR2 overexpression promotes kallikrein-related peptidase 5 (KLK5) release through a calcium-dependent pathway ( ). This may explain why patients respond strongly to environmental stimuli. KLK5 is a serine protease that processes the cathelicidin precursor into the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide (LL-37), which in turn activates inflammatory responses; these steps were first established in skin and keratinocytes from patients with rosacea ( ). Temperature changes, ultraviolet exposure, microbial products, and dietary factors can repeatedly activate the same pathway, which offers a molecular explanation for why the same triggers cause repeated episodes at the same site. Treatment with azelaic acid 15% gel for 16 weeks reduced cathelicidin and KLK5 expression and serine protease activity (SPA) in lesional skin, with TLR2 suppression observed in mouse skin ( ). A small RCT showed that a topical serine protease inhibitor lowered SPA and that the reduction correlated with improvement in severity ( ). Mast cells are key effectors of this axis. After intradermal injection of LL-37, mast-cell-deficient mice do not develop rosacea-like changes; mast-cell stabilizers downregulate matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP9) and C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CXCL2); and in patients with erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, 8 weeks of topical cromoglycate reduced MMP activity in lesions ( ). Recent mechanistic studies have identified several receptors through which LL-37 activates mast cells: TLR2 with downstream Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/STAT3 signaling ( ), the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2) in humans and its mouse ortholog, Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor B2 (MRGPRB2) ( , ), and mitochondrial DNA release with cyclic GMP-AMP synthase/stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS/STING) pathway activation ( ). Mast-cell-derived mediators also act on vascular endothelium and sensory nerves, linking immune amplification to neurovascular symptoms such as flushing and burning ( , , ). In this way, the axis and neurogenic inflammation reinforce each other and jointly contribute to the chronicity network. At the same time, the causal position of mast cells should not be overstated. In a comparative histopathological study of 20 Korean patients, lesional inflammatory mediator expression did not differ significantly between mast cell-rich and mast cell-poor rosacea skin (interleukin-6 (IL-6), P = 0.519; LL-37, P = 0.443; TNF-α, P = 0.400) ( ). Mast cells may thus be an important amplifier rather than a sufficient or universal determinant of lesional inflammation, and their contribution may vary across subtypes and disease phases. Neuroimmune interactions may be an important component of the sensitized state. Sensory neurons contribute to flushing and neurogenic inflammation through transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and other ion channels; TRPV1-nerve growth factor (NGF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TrkA) signaling is activated in rosacea skin and is further exacerbated by Demodex mites ( ). text: Evidence consistent with inflammatory memory in rosacea: activated receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1)-expressing γδ T cells to produce IL-17A; γδ T cells were increased in rosacea lesions, and genetic depletion of γδ T cells or CGRP receptor antagonism reduced rosacea-like dermatitis ( ). In patients, serum CGRP levels differed between neurogenic and non-neurogenic rosacea, supporting a clinically relevant neurogenic endotype ( ). Peripheral blood from 280 patients with rosacea showed elevated interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-17, and interleukin-8 (IL-8) that correlated positively with anxiety and depression ( ). These observations link neural, innate, and adaptive components into a recurrent activation circuit, but whether the neuroimmune loop itself stores memory or merely amplifies pre-existing memory remains unknown. Similarly, whether mast cells themselves acquire a long-lived primed state after repeated LL-37 stimulation, analogous to trained immunity in macrophages, remains untested and warrants direct functional study. More direct evidence for persistence comes from tissue-level omics studies. A paired transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of lesional and non-lesional tissue from five patients with papulopustular rosacea showed significant upregulation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and TNF pathways centered on IL-1β. text: Evidence consistent with inflammatory memory in rosacea: suggesting that the inflammatory program of lesional skin may pre-exist in normal-appearing skin and can be re-primed by a single cytokine. This pattern is consistent with a “program + trigger” memory-like model. However, the sample size was small, the experiment was ex vivo, and the exogenous IL-1β concentration may not reflect physiological levels. These results suggest, but do not prove, that a re-primable inflammatory program exists in non-lesional skin. Integrated proteomic, phosphoproteomic, and transcriptomic analyses further support the coexistence of immune-inflammatory and neurovascular programs in rosacea skin ( , ). In summary, the TLR2→KLK5→LL-37→mast cell/IL-1β axis has positive-feedback and self-maintaining features and is the most plausible candidate for an inflammatory memory-like state in rosacea. These features may explain why the same triggers repeatedly induce episodes at the same site; however, whether the pathway persists in a residual state between episodes remains unsupported by longitudinal molecular evidence. The evidence currently remains at the level of molecular pathways, and direct verification through human lesional epigenomic or single-cell studies is still lacking.

text: Relapse after treatment withdrawal: treatment-dependent remission and relapse kinetics: Relapse after treatment withdrawal is a relatively consistent memory-like phenomenon in clinical studies of rosacea. Multiple RCTs and cohort studies show that maintenance therapy reduces relapse rates, whereas relapse after withdrawal occurs within weeks to months ( – ). This indicates that remission depends largely on continuous suppression of inflammation rather than on true resetting of tissue programs. The time to relapse after withdrawal is quantifiable and reproducible across studies, making it a candidate observational metric for disease-modification endpoints. This clinical pattern is consistent with a locally retained, reactivatable inflammatory program, but it does not by itself prove the existence of tissue memory; current therapies still aim mainly at controlling active symptoms. Most existing relapse assessments rely on physician-assessed lesion recurrence and pay insufficient attention to subjective symptoms such as flushing and burning or to changes in trigger thresholds; predictive factors for relapse have not been established. In a prospective study of 60 patients with papulopustular rosacea treated with ivermectin 1% cream for 16 weeks, 70% (42/60) achieved an Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score of 0. text: Relapse after treatment withdrawal: treatment-dependent remission and relapse kinetics: relapse rate during follow-up was 45.24%, with most relapses being mild (IGA 1) ( ). This study used relapse kinetics as its main outcome and shows that the time to relapse after withdrawal is quantifiable and can serve as a candidate disease-course endpoint; however, it was a single-arm observational study with a small sample and did not establish predictive factors for relapse. A real-world Japanese cohort of 42 patients followed for 1 year further showed that physician- and patient-reported severity measures declined over time, indicating that longitudinal disease-course outcomes are feasible in routine practice ( ).

text: Non-lesional “program-trigger” evidence and relapse threshold indicators: Non-lesional tissue studies provide preliminary evidence that the memory extends beyond lesional boundaries. Non-lesional tissue explants can be re-primed by IL-1β into a lesional-like state ( ). TLR2 overexpression in lesional epidermis ( ) further points to enhanced keratinocyte responsiveness to environmental stimuli, although it does not establish that non-lesional skin shares this phenotype. Trigger-burden assessment is a practical way to quantify this threshold clinically. In a prospective case-control study of 100 patients with rosacea and 100 controls, hot bathing habits were significantly more common in the rosacea group (P = 0.011), and heat, sunlight, emotional stress, alcohol, and spicy food were the most frequently reported triggers ( ). Standardized trigger diaries or trigger-burden scores could therefore be used to track whether the minimum stimulus intensity required to induce an episode decreases over time, a prediction that follows directly from the memory model (Section 5).

text: Cross-disease mechanistic evidence for drivers of recurrence: Because direct evidence in rosacea is limited, mechanistic studies from other chronic skin diseases help clarify how the three categories of inflammatory memory may drive recurrence. These studies provide analogies and design templates, not proof of the same mechanisms in rosacea. Psoriasis provides relatively complete TRM evidence for same-site recurrence. Epidermal CD8 + TRM and Th22/Tc17 cells persist long-term in resolved lesions and can secrete pathogenic factors ( ); the pathogenic T cells are present as oligoclonally expanded clones ( ); and the IL-17A-dominated response elicited by resident T-cell activation predicts early relapse after withdrawal of phototherapy ( ). These results indicate that even after complete clinical resolution, pathogenic T cells can remain resident and drive recurrence at the same site. Pathogenic clones are also found in non-lesional skin ( ), indicating that memory T cells can pre-exist in clinically normal areas. Once reactivated by environmental or local factors, they may contribute to the formation of new or recurrent lesions. In rosacea, direct evidence for skin-resident T cells has only recently emerged. text: Cross-disease mechanistic evidence for drivers of recurrence: ( ). An immunohistochemical study also showed altered CD4/CD8 T-cell ratios and CD123 + plasmacytoid dendritic cells in rosacea compared with discoid lupus erythematosus and polymorphous light eruption ( ). Two important caveats apply. First, T-cell infiltrates in rosacea are generally sparse and less dense than in psoriasis, so the demonstration of resident memory populations does not establish that they drive relapse. Second, these data are cross-sectional; the cells could be bystanders recruited by ongoing inflammation rather than the memory carriers of the model. Whether resident-cell abundance is associated with relapse risk in rosacea remains unknown. Functional studies, such as quantification of clonal expansion, reactivation-induced IL-17A release from sorted resident cells, and longitudinal correlation of resident-cell abundance with time to relapse, are needed before the TRM layer can be accepted in rosacea.

text: The epithelial/non-immune cell memory layer: Epithelial cells can also retain disease memory. Epidermal keratinocytes isolated from resolved psoriatic lesions retain disease-related transcriptomic features and 5-methylcytosine (5-mC)/5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5-hmC) epigenetic changes, with enrichment of WNT/TNF/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathways ( ). Mechanistic studies of airway epithelial progenitors ( ), epidermal stem cells ( ), and synovial fibroblasts ( ) further indicate that inflammation can write reactivatable chromatin programs into non-immune cells. Epithelial memory is not an irreversible all-or-nothing switch. Airway epithelial progenitors maintain transcriptional memory after IL-4/IL-13 withdrawal ( ), showing that such memory can be retained long-term, and epidermal stem cells remain in a poised state through long-term open chromatin regions ( ). Interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-induced transcriptional memory further shows that establishment and maintenance can be controlled by different mechanisms: establishment requires signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), whereas maintenance is STAT1-independent, and the memory is inherited through cell division as chromatin changes and can be reversed ( ). Establishment, maintenance, and recall can therefore be targeted separately, which provides a molecular basis for staged therapy.

text: The trained immunity layer: Trained immunity can either promote or inhibit tissue damage depending on the direction of the response ( ). Repeated TLR2/LL-37 stimulation in rosacea could theoretically retrain local macrophages, and a mechanistic study in mice showed that guanylate-binding protein 5 (GBP5) promotes rosacea-like inflammation by skewing macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype through the NF-κB pathway ( ). However, direct evidence in human skin innate immune cells remains lacking. The same macrophage population can differentiate toward pro-fibrotic or anti-fibrotic phenotypes under different training conditions, and the phenotype can be retained after adoptive transfer ( ). If trained immunity operates in rosacea, the therapeutic goal would be to steer it rather than simply deplete it, although this remains a conceptual inference at present.

text: Cellular and molecular basis of relapse after treatment withdrawal: Drug clearance is an expected component of relapse after treatment withdrawal, but the reproducible timing of relapse and the re-emergence of specific inflammatory programs suggest that withdrawal relapse is not simply passive restoration of baseline inflammation. After withdrawal of an anti-CD11a monoclonal antibody, relapsing psoriatic lesions show T-cell reinfiltration and increases in inflammatory myeloid dendritic cells expressing TNF/inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)/TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) ( ). After withdrawal of the interleukin-23 (IL-23) inhibitor guselkumab, serum IL-17A/F and IL-22 rise at the time of relapse, with the cytokine increase lagging behind the clinical recurrence ( ). Molecular programs are thus reactivated at the time of relapse; whether tissue molecular changes precede clinically detectable recurrence remains to be tested in longitudinal studies. A 12-year multicenter cohort of 991 treatment episodes further showed that each additional prior treatment withdrawal increased the risk of relapse by approximately 23%, and that the speed of relapse differed across biologics with different mechanisms ( ). These findings suggest that repeated withdrawal-relapse cycles may accumulate a relapse-prone state. text: A hypothetical multilayer memory network model: Based on the evidence above, we propose a hypothetical integrated model ( ). External triggers first activate the TLR2/KLK5/LL-37 axis, and inflammation is then amplified through mast cells and IL-1β ( , , , ). Repeated episodes write multilayer memory into the skin: epigenetic imprints in keratinocytes and stem cells ( , ), directional training of macrophages ( , ), local residency of pathogenic T cells ( – , ), and fibroblast remodeling ( ). Nerve-ending sensitization and changes in ion-channel activity are included as a memory-adjacent amplifier rather than as direct evidence of inflammatory memory ( , , , ). These memories jointly lower the relapse threshold, which clinically manifests as treatment-dependent remission ( – ). The core prediction of the model is a lowered relapse threshold: the stimulus intensity required to induce an episode decreases with repeated inflammation. Repeated inflammation leaves the skin with low-level background activation during clinical quiescence, so that previously tolerated stimuli can cross the episode threshold. Treatment suppresses active inflammation and maintains clinical remission but may not erase memory traces; after withdrawal, the threshold therefore quickly returns to a level at which episodes occur. Second, withdrawal studies show that molecular programs are reactivated at the time of relapse: relapsing psoriatic lesions show T-cell reinfiltration and inflammatory dendritic-cell activation ( ), and serum cytokines rise at the time of relapse rather than before it ( ); whether molecular changes precede clinically detectable recurrence remains untested. Third, the idea that repeated relapse accumulates susceptibility derives from a psoriasis cohort, in which more prior treatment withdrawals were associated with higher relapse risk ( ). Direct evidence in rosacea currently covers only the first pillar and is limited to a small ex vivo study; the complete multilayer memory network should therefore remain a hypothesis to be tested. To make the model testable, we propose an operational definition of the relapse threshold. We define the relapse threshold as the minimum stimulus intensity, or the cumulative trigger burden, required to induce a clinical episode in a given patient. A lowered threshold would then manifest as one or more of the following: a shorter time to relapse after withdrawal, relapse after milder or fewer triggers, and a greater cumulative number or severity of episodes per unit time. A meaningful threshold shift should ultimately be calibrated against the minimal clinically important difference of validated rosacea severity measures and against prespecified disease-course changes (for example, a prolongation of relapse-free time or a reduction in trigger burden exceeding the measurement error of the diary), with replication in an independent cohort; we deliberately do not assign a numeric value at this stage because no calibration data exist in rosacea. A further testable feature of the model is its hierarchical structure. If epithelial/stem-cell memory forms the long-term layer, trained immunity the intermediate layer, and TRM the local rapid effector layer, different therapeutic strategies should act on different layers. This ordering does not imply equal evidence weight: in rosacea, direct support is currently strongest for the re-primable non-lesional program ( ), whereas the TRM layer is the least supported and requires functional and longitudinal validation ( ). Combination or sequential therapy may come closer than single-target therapy to the goal of rewriting memory.

text: Abstract: Abstract Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that primarily affects the central facial region, including the cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead. Its clinical features include episodic flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, papulopustular lesions, and in severe cases, phymatous changes such as rhinophyma. Rosacea substantially impairs patients’ quality of life, while current treatments focus primarily on symptom control. The pathogenesis of this disease involves abnormal immune responses, infiltration of immune cells, inflammatory reactions and angiogenesis, etc. Post-translational modifications (PTMs), particularly phosphorylation and ubiquitination, may play a role in initiating and sustaining these processes. This article reviews how PTMs such as phosphorylation and ubiquitination affect the pathogenesis of rosacea and assesses these PTM-regulated pathways as potential therapeutic targets. Keywords: biomarkers, phosphorylation, post-translational modification, rosacea, ubiquitination and acetylation

text: Introduction: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that predominantly affects the central area of the face, presenting as recurrent flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, papules, and pustules. In severe cases, hypertrophic changes such as rhinophyma may occur ( ). This condition is more prevalent among middle-aged people, with a global prevalence of approximately 5% ( ). The onset of rosacea is influenced by multiple factors, including genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, abnormal neurovascular regulation, and an imbalance in innate immune function ( ). Pathologically, rosacea is characterized by chronic inflammation and vasodilation of the facial skin. Patients often report sensory abnormalities such as burning and stinging, which significantly affect their quality of life and mental health. Some patients may also experience complications, including anxiety and depression. Currently, recognized treatments for rosacea are limited and often ineffective, leading to frequent relapses. Recent studies have identified key molecular pathways and inflammatory networks in rosacea, including innate immune responses regulated by PTMs ( ). Despite this potential connection, the precise role of post-translational modifications in rosacea remains unclear, hindering the development of targeted therapies. Further elucidation of these mechanisms and translational research is necessary. Accordingly, we conducted a literature review, searching extensively for articles on rosacea and its related post-translational modifications. Our goal was to identify pathways closely associated with rosacea that may have potential applications in treatment. text: Aetiology and pathogenesis of rosacea: The pathogenesis of rosacea results from the interaction between genetic predispositions and environmental factors. Evidence of familial aggregation and susceptibility in specific populations suggests the presence of genetic risk factors ( ). For example, certain human leukocyte antigen subtypes and the cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide gene, which encodes the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin, may be linked to the disease’s susceptibility ( ). Environmental triggers, such as ultraviolet radiation, heat stimulation, emotional stress, spicy foods, alcohol, and microbial imbalances like Demodex mites, are known to exacerbate the condition ( ). These external stimuli can trigger an inflammatory cascade and vasodilation in rosacea through post-translational modification mechanisms (e.g., phosphorylation and ubiquitination), leading to abnormal facial skin reactions. Epidermal keratinocytes play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of rosacea by sensing environmental triggers and amplifying innate immune responses ( ). Increased expression of Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) has been detected in keratinocytes within rosacea lesions, which may enhance cutaneous sensitivity to microbial products, ultraviolet radiation, temperature changes, and other external stimuli ( ). text: Immune cell infiltration and inflammatory pathways in rosacea: A variety of immune cells infiltrate rosacea lesions, collectively shaping a complex inflammatory microenvironment ( ). Among these cells, macrophages are particularly enriched in the dermis and are increasingly recognised as key effector cells in sustaining chronic cutaneous inflammation ( ). Histological analyses of rosacea lesions have frequently demonstrated marked infiltration of macrophages and monocytes, especially around dermal blood vessels ( ). Notably, macrophages in rosacea tend to acquire a classically activated M1-like phenotype ( ). These M1 macrophages produce abundant pro-inflammatory mediators, including IL-1β, IL-18, and TNF-α, thereby contributing to tissue damage, immune amplification, and angiogenesis ( ). Experimental studies further support a functional role for macrophages in rosacea-like inflammation. Macrophage depletion attenuates LL-37-induced rosacea-like skin inflammation in mice, suggesting that macrophages are not merely bystander cells but active drivers of disease pathology. Transcriptomic analyses have identified guanylate-binding protein 5 (GBP5) as significantly upregulated in rosacea tissues, with its expression positively correlated with macrophage infiltration. text: Immune cell infiltration and inflammatory pathways in rosacea: direct cytokine production, but also through regulation of keratinocyte kinase signalling, inflammasome activation, and angiogenic responses. Mast cells, which are widely distributed around dermal blood vessels, also play a distinctive role in rosacea pathogenesis ( ). They represent an important source of LL-37 and KLK5, the serine protease responsible for cleaving cathelicidin into its active peptide form ( ). Muto et al. demonstrated that mast cells are critical mediators of cathelicidin-driven inflammation, as LL-37 induces mast-cell activation and degranulation, leading to the release of histamine, chemokines, and matrix metalloproteinases ( ). In mast cell-deficient mice, LL-37 injection fails to induce typical rosacea-like inflammation, further underscoring the essential contribution of mast cells to LL-37-mediated cutaneous inflammation ( ). Several phosphorylation-dependent pathways appear to regulate mast-cell activation in rosacea. LL-37-induced mast-cell activation and degranulation are accompanied by increased phosphorylation of JAK2 and STAT3, as well as elevated expression of TLR2 and myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88). GE1111, an antagonist of MAS-related G protein-coupled receptor X2/B2 (MRGPRX2/B2), inhibits the MRGPRX2-mediated mast-cell activation pathway by reducing stromal interaction molecule 1 expression and ERK1/2 phosphorylation ( ).

In animal models, topical cyclosporine A or SP23 suppresses cGAS/STING/NF-κB signalling in dermal mast cells and ameliorates rosacea-like dermatitis ( ). These findings suggest that mast cells may amplify rosacea inflammation through both LL-37-dependent degranulation and mitochondrial DNA-driven innate immune activation. The TLR7/NF-κB/mTORC1 axis enhances the production of cytokines and chemokines, thereby facilitating the recruitment of CD4+ T cells into rosacea lesions ( ). text: Immune cell infiltration and inflammatory pathways in rosacea: of NF-κB activation. The TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB pathway amplifies LL-37-induced inflammatory responses and is closely linked to dysregulated innate immunity in rosacea ( ). In response to inflammatory stimuli, NAD-dependent deacetylase sirtuin 7 (SIRT7) promotes TLR2 upregulation, thereby further enhancing NF-κB pathway activation ( ). Thus, both the TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB and SIRT7–TLR2–NF-κB axes may represent potential therapeutic targets for controlling excessive innate immune activation in rosacea. Additional regulatory molecules and therapeutic candidates further converge on NF-κB-related inflammatory signalling. Overexpression of DnaJ heat shock protein family member B2 (DNAJB2) alleviates rosacea-like skin damage and suppresses the expression of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and angiogenic mediators. DNAJB2 also inhibits endoplasmic reticulum stress marker proteins and suppresses activation of the TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB phosphorylation cascade. Moreover, DNAJB2 overexpression reduces CD4+ T-cell infiltration and downregulates genes associated with T helper 1 (Th1) and T helper 17 (Th17) polarisation ( ). Quercetin-loaded cellulose nanocrystals (QL-CNCs) similarly attenuate LL-37-induced rosacea-like inflammation, reducing erythema, inflammatory infiltration, mast-cell activation, and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, while inhibiting Th1/Th17 immune polarisation.

The therapeutic effects of QL-CNCs are abolished by NF-κB activator 1, confirming the central role of this pathway ( ). Minocycline also inhibits inflammatory-cell infiltration and cytokine production in rosacea-like mouse skin and cellular models. Mechanistically, minocycline blocks LL-37-induced TLR4/TNF-α activation, downregulates TLR4 and phosphorylated NF-κB, and reduces ROS production ( ). Similarly, artemisinin inhibits LL-37-induced NF-κB activation and NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation in HaCaT cells ( ). text: Neurovascular factors and other mechanisms: Another prominent feature of rosacea is recurrent flushing and persistent vasodilation, which are thought to arise from abnormal neurovascular regulation ( ). Facial skin is densely innervated by sensory nerve fibres, and these nerves appear to be hyper-responsive in rosacea. Increased expression of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, particularly transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4), has been observed in sensory nerves and mast cells in rosacea lesions ( , ). Environmental and chemical stimuli, including temperature changes and capsaicin, may activate TRP channels and induce the release of neurogenic inflammatory mediators, such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). These mediators promote vasodilation, vascular hyperreactivity, and inflammatory amplification, thereby linking sensory-nerve activation to the characteristic erythema and flushing of rosacea ( ). In addition to functional vasodilation, enhanced angiogenesis has been observed in rosacea lesions and in LL-37-induced rosacea-like mouse models. Pharmacological inhibition of angiogenesis attenuates LL-37-induced rosacea-like manifestations, suggesting that vascular remodelling is not merely a secondary consequence of inflammation but may actively contribute to disease persistence. Inhibition of endothelial mTORC1 reduces angiogenesis and protects mice from rosacea-like inflammation, whereas excessive mTORC1 activation promotes vascular proliferation and aggravates rosacea-like phenotypes. Consistently, in vitro studies have shown that blockade of mTORC1 signalling markedly suppresses LL-37-induced tube formation in human endothelial cells. Phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6, a downstream marker of mTORC1 activation, appears to mediate this angiogenic response ( ).

text: Post-translational modifications and rosacea: In rosacea, immune dysregulation is characterised by the amplification of phosphorylation-dependent signalling cascades across multiple cellular compartments and inflammatory pathways ( ). Among the post-translational modifications implicated in rosacea, phosphorylation has been the most extensively investigated. STAT3 phosphorylation is markedly increased in rosacea lesions and has been reported to correlate with interleukin-36γ (IL-36γ) expression. Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation attenuates inflammatory responses in both in vitro and in vivo models, suggesting that the STAT3/IL-36γ axis may represent a potential therapeutic target ( ). Consistently, enhanced STAT3 activation in rosacea lesions has been associated with sustained upstream stimulation by cytokines such as IL-6 and with the induction of downstream pro-angiogenic genes ( ). Single-cell RNA sequencing has further identified a distinct keratinocyte subset in rosacea lesions characterised by impaired barrier function and enrichment of interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-related signalling. Blockade of IFN-γ signalling alleviates inflammation, supporting the involvement of IFN-γ-driven phosphorylation events, particularly the JAK/STAT pathway, in rosacea pathogenesis ( ). In rosacea cell models, phosphorylation levels of ERK1/2 and p38 are significantly elevated compared with controls and are associated with increased expression of pro-inflammatory mediators and stress-response genes, including IL-18 ( ). In mast cells, LL-37 activates MAS-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2), leading to ERK1/2 and NF-κB phosphorylation, which in turn promotes inflammatory mediator release and immune-cell chemotaxis ( ). The p38 pathway may further amplify inflammation by upregulating cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF and by modulating enzymes such as inducible nitric oxide synthase, thereby increasing the production of nitric oxide and other inflammatory mediators ( ). Importantly, phosphorylation is not uniformly pro-inflammatory; it is also constrained by endogenous negative feedback mechanisms. Under sustained stimulation, phosphatases such as mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase 1 can be induced to dephosphorylate and inactivate p38 and JNK, thereby limiting the duration and intensity of inflammatory signalling ( ).
